# Preface

The Proceeding includes the research contribution from the International Conference on Next-Gen Technologies in Computational Intelligence (NGTCA 2023) held on March 24th 2023 at Vels Institute of Science, Technology and Advanced Studies. NGCTA 2023 is the flagship conference of the Computer Society of India (Region 7). Computer Society of India (CSI) is the largest association of IT professionals in India. CSI is a non-profit organization established in 1965 and its members are committed to the advancement of theory and practice of Computer Engineering and Technology Systems. The Mission of CSI is to facilitate research, knowledge sharing, learning, and career enhancement for all categories of IT professionals, while simultaneously inspiring and nurturing new entrants into the industry and helping them to integrate into the IT community. At present, CSI has 76chapters across India, over 550 student branches with 1,00,000 plus members. It serves its members through technical events, seminars, workshops, conferences, publications & journals, research projects, competitions, special interest groups, awards & recognitions, etc. Various CSI chapters conduct Research Convention every year.

This year, nine chapters in Region 7, namely, Chennai, Kancheepuram, Trivandrum, Sivakasi, Coimbatore, Trichy, Vellore, Salem & Cochin along with Vels Institute of Science, Technology and Advanced Studies, Chennai organized the International Research Convention on Next-Gen Technologies in Computational Intelligence. The international conference is focused on research and emphasizes the latest technological advancements in Computational Intelligence. The conference aims to provide awareness in the area of intelligent technologies to analyze emerging trends and new findings. The platform helped to explore and share cutting-edge research thereby triggering collaborative research.

It showcased the commitment of the Computer Society of India in bringing together various disciplines, converging and amalgamating various new ideas, fields, and technologies. It brought academia, researchers, and practitioners with similar or varied interests on a common platform to explore, reflect, and rediscover the new frontiers of knowledge and technology in the field of Computational intelligence. The increase in computing power and sensor data accelerated the research in Data Analytics. The conference bundled with technical talk educated the audience.

The meticulous planning for the conference started around 10 months back and the nine chapters ensured quality in compiling the research contributions. The core committee meticulously planned and executed the conference with utmost care. The conference strictly adheres to screen-quality papers on the theme. The submitted papers are subject to a peer review process to be selected for publishing articles meeting high standards in intelligent technologies. Out of the 300 papers submitted, only 80 papers were selected for oral presentation after a rigorous review. Besides paper presentations, the conference also showcased plenary talks by experts in the respective field. The editors would like to acknowledge all the authors for their contributions. We appreciate the unconditional support by the

CSI chapters under Region 7. We hope the proceedings will provide the state of the art knowledge in the field of intelligent technologies. The research contributions will inspire and accelerate new knowledge in the field.

# Foreword

I am happy to write this Foreword for the Proceedings of the International Research conference on Next-Gen technologies \[NGCTI 2023\] at the organized by the Computer Society of India Region 7 withthe Kancheepuram Chapter in the lead. We are in the first half of the third decade of the 21st century, widely acclaimed as India’s millennium. The progress in India in recent years in leveraging digital technologies for larger public good is globally acclaimed both in terms of scale and reach. These developments are touching the lives of a large number of ordinary citizens and businesses. The underlying enablers are connectivity, mobile penetration, and interoperability of systems - mostly technologies pioneered during 199x to 201x. The echo system of innovation, entrepreneurship and start-ups for nurture and support are now in place and with growth, these will push forward greater adoption of next-gen technologies through multiplier-effects of combining them for improved solutions in many segments including finance, governance, retail, logistics, regulatory compliance, education, health and G2C services.

Artificial Intelligence driven by deep-learning, Large-language generative models and their applications in diverse fields, Augmented and Virtual Reality, Internet-of-things, 5G-6G, quantum computing and quantum computers, digital biology — are some of the emerging technologies where we may expect substantive break-throughs in the coming decades in terms of wide-spread and large-scale adoption. Harnessing of the potential of these next-gen technologies to greatly enhance education, health and security requires policy, public-private synergy and a climate of peace. The challenge is in transforming businesses, organizations and society from as-is to to-become and to-be. The technologies also have the possibility of wrong and misuse and these require effective regulatory framework a priori rather than a-posteriori. A participatory process is essential to make this happen. We need to prepare and have work-force with skills and attitude, especially ability for continuous life-long learning, to be the change agents of this talent-transformation.

The conference has refereed papers authored by faculty, students, researchers and industry professionals. The papers indicate a wide range of problems and applications addressing solutions for problems of interest to various stake holders and organizations. It is noteworthy that the proceedings are published and brought out for greater reach and sharing.

# Blockchain-Based Identity Management System in the Digital Industry

D. Gayathri^([¹](#fn1))

E-mail: [gayathri.dl992@gmail.com](mailto:gayathri.dl992@gmail.com), [raghavendran.scs@velsuniv.ac.in](mailto:raghavendran.scs@velsuniv.ac.in)

DOI: [10.1201/9781003430452-1](https://dx.doi.org/10.1201/9781003430452-1)

## Abstract

Blockchain Identity Management plays a vital role in the verification and validation of documents while transferring between servers. For all the records in an entity verifications and validations are carried out in Blockchain Identity Management. By providing a decentralized system identity theft can be avoided. A decentralized system that allows only the user to access the documents after the validation and verification process is made and then the personal details will be shared with the concerned user. This survey discusses the identity concepts of Blockchain identity management used in the Digital industry.

***Keywords:*** Blockchain, Digital Identity, Blockchain Identity Management, Self-sovereign, Blockchain classification

## Introduction

In the 21 st century, the biggest innovation can be the emergence of Blockchain in the digital world, it has many concepts to handle the security and privacy challenges (Chatterjee, 2017) faced in the digital era using Blockchain Identity Management. This paper gives a clear picture overview of Blockchain Technology (Ramachandran and Krishnamachari, 2018), Blockchain Classification, Self-sovereign Identity Model, Blockchain in Digital Identity, and the most widespread technologies of Blockchain Identity Management systems like uPort, Sovrin, and ShoCard.

## Overview of the Blockchain

Blockchain, a shared ledger ([Liu et al., 2020](#ch1.xhtml#ref1_26)) allows millions of computers and servers to conserve a secured, single, immutable ledger. Blockchain is controlled by the network participants using a consensus mechanism without having any central authority. Blockchain is a network (Jamal et al., 2019) technology that allows users to distribute information safely and to ensure point-to-point transactions without any central authority.

It is like a conventional public ledger that holds the complete list of the transaction history. AllBlocks contains a block header and block body. Validation rules are indicated by the Block version. SHA256 (parent block header) computes the previous hash value (Jamal et al., 2019) and is referred to as Parent Block Hash. SHA256 also computes the Merkle root tree Hash value of the communications in the block which is Merkle Tree Root. The first block is the Genesis Block which doesn’t has any previous block. For verification, all blocks will trace the Genesis Block.

## Blockchain Strengths

The promising features of Blockchain Technology ([Li et al., 2020](#ch1.xhtml#ref1_3)) are as follows:

### 1\. Decentralized

Blockchain gives equal rights to all parties to access the complete database and all records ([Nofer et al., 2017](#ch1.xhtml#ref1_14)). No one particular party controls the entire database, everyone has full rights.

### 2\. Security

In Blockchain each node will store all the data, everyone has a ledger, and no threats will be affected if any node is damaged or affected.

### 3\. Distributed nature

The identical blockchain data will be deposited between many users at the equivalent time, if suddenly a node gets affected or another misses the data the other nodes in the blockchain network have the same copy of the blockchain and it will be updated automatically. This feature avoids data loss, and tamper records.

### 4\. Transparency and traceability

Everyone in the network can be able to check and eyeshot all the activities and transactions because Blockchain records (Mohammed, 2021) are deposited on full nodes with timestamps. All the activities and Transactions could be traced by the address of the node hence blockchain is traceable and transparent ([Syed et al., 2019](#ch1.xhtml#ref1_15)). It also helps in fraud detection.

### 5\. Efficiency

Removal of intermediary subsystems in Blockchain by allowing the systems to work with more efficiency autonomously ([Mohanta et al., 2018](#ch1.xhtml#ref1_19)).

## Blockchain Classification

### 1\. Permissionless or public Blockchain

Anyone can interact or join the network without any permission and begin submitting documents. The core of digital currencies trade in the open-source results like Ethereum (Mohammed 2021) and Bitcoin is achieved only by this category.

### 2\. Permission or private Blockchain

This sealed infrastructure requires pre-verification ([Liu et al., 2020](#ch1.xhtml#ref1_26)) for the undertaking parties in the Blockchain network, only confined users can validate the block transaction. Thus, Permissioned Blockchain is used to increase internal business control are preferred by centralized organizations.

### 3\. Consortium Blockchain

Here the consensus procedure is managed by the preferred group of participants and this sort of blockchain is partially private (Jamal et al., 2019). The other public participants are restricted to read the Blockchain data.

![Fig. 1.1. Blockchain Classification](images/fig1_1_C.jpg)

Fig. 1.1. Blockchain Classification

Blockchain-Based Identity Management System in the Digital Industry

### 4\. Hybrid Blockchain

Hashed data blocks are created by using private blockchain networks (Mohammed, 2021) and then the data is saved by a private (Mohammed, 2021) blockchain network.

## Blockchain in Digital Identity

Digital Identity is used to refer to a particular individual uniquely to identify using digital information and to have a face-to-face transaction that would ensure a good confidence level between two or more parties ([Lim et al., 2018](#ch1.xhtml#ref1_6)). Digital Identities are stored using a Blockchain decentralized database that has no admin. Blockchain data are immutable, so no one has access to change it (Li, 2020). The digital industry spends more money on data security capabilities. But Hackers easily cross all the securities (Raikwar, 2019). Administrative Privilege control, Record encryption, and Tokenization are the main factors that ensure the security of the database (Balasubramaniam, 2020). All these main factors and the security of the data are managed by Blockchain Technology. Blockchain decentralized system plays a crucial role in Digital Information Storage.

They store digital identities based on the attributes that are deposited in the database and that differentiate users of the same system ([Liu et al., 2020](#ch1.xhtml#ref1_26)). Static attributes like date of birth, and gender and dynamic attributes like age, designation, and so on. We have some specific identifiers called attributes of a person like a passport number, email address, etc ([Faber et al., 2019](#ch1.xhtml#ref1_8)). For online services, the common attribute of a person is the Email address for all the individuals.

## Self-Sovereign Identity Model

Self-sovereign identity is that no third party ([Raju et al., 2017](#ch1.xhtml#ref1_10)) jurisdiction dominates the identity only the user has complete control over the identity. This model helps to manage the digital identities of an individual (Mohammed, 2021). While the individual has the sole ownership over the ability to manage the personal data and to deny access to the other third party.

## Blockchain Identity Management Systems

### Sovrin

In the offline world (Rafique, 2021), Sovrin is designed to use digital credentials safely. Since it has a self-sovereign identity so, it cannot be eliminated and does not depend on any central authority. To ensure privacy it acquires knowledge-free proof encryption.

## uPort

It is an open system (Raju, 2017) that gives self-sovereign identities to the users and organization. The uPort identity system works on the Ethereum blockchain to identify a user or organization digitally and to join assertions.

## ShoCard

The users will hold and secure their digital identities (Mohammed, 2021). The users will have a user key to ensure privacy, by which a third-party database can be eliminated ([Lim et al., 2018](#ch1.xhtml#ref1_6)). ShoCard has the confirmation message of the user on Blockchain (Haddouti and Kettani, 2019), which will provide the reliability of (Ramachandran and Krishnamachari, 2018) user personal identity and improve (Verma, 2021) third-party verification.

## Problems with Blockchain in Digital Identity

The Problems with Blockchain in Digital Identity (Haddouti and Kettani, 2019) may be based on two key elements like user believes the identification provider (Jamal et al., 2019), and similarly, the provider of the service ([Li et al., 2020](#ch1.xhtml#ref1_3)) believes the provider of the identity (Mohammed, 2021). For instance, a vicious provider of identity (Mohammed, 2021) can easily access the service provider, using the (Mohammed, 2021) user’s identity (Verma, 2021) without their knowledge. This unauthorized access may not be identified by the user. Therefore, the change in system design (Ishmaev, 2020) should be done So that the identity provider should be notified by the service provider when a new (Balasubramaniam, 2020) provider is joined to the domain. Another problem ([Sanka et al., 2020](#ch1.xhtml#ref1_16)) might be access given to the resources of different types, Access approval should be done by the administrative staff to avoid mis happenings in an organization.

## Conclusion

Analysis of Blockchain-based identity system based on identity verification ([Faber et al., 2019](#ch1.xhtml#ref1_8)) that is completely accessed by the individual ([Raju et al., 2017](#ch1.xhtml#ref1_10)) user to increase the trust in data quality and reliability. As a pare review, we have observed enormous challenges related to block data storage, different users, and their storage capabilities. Another one is related to the deauthorization category in the blockchain. Few nodes only participate while many others can only view the block data. Thus, Blockchain Based Identity Management systems overcome enormous limitations when compared to conventional Identity Management systems. Hence the user becomes their identity owner and not requires the user to self-sacrifice safety for comfort. On this digital world, Identity Management can be more efficient and secure to do all communications safely. To ignore data breaches by the services and applications Blockchain-based Identity Management allows user to manage their own identity by placing it in a decentralized system. Hence more efforts are needed to build a perfect view to preserve the data privacy challenges of Blockchain Identity Management systems.

# An Improved Neural Network Classifier for Melanoma Skin Lesion Detection

Dr. T. D. Srividya

Assistant Professor, Department of Computer Science, St. Anne’s Arts & Science College, Madhavaram, Chennai

E-mail: [saividyamurthy@gmail.com](mailto:saividyamurthy@gmail.com)

DOI: [10.1201/9781003430452-2](https://dx.doi.org/10.1201/9781003430452-2)

## Abstract

Segmentation and categorization of skin cancer play a major role in pattern recognition. CAD methods are used nowadays for the initial diagnosis of skin cancer detection. Performing medicinal imagery segmentation besides classification with a deep learning model establishes training on a large dataset. Two datasets are proposed for this work. The present work focuses on an automated skin lesion discovery system to categorize the form of skin cancer, benign, and malignant. Several segmentation algorithms are used. An innovative feature extraction algorithm is projected in the present work. These features become an input to the SCG classifier. The classification accuracy of our projected system is estimated based on SCG Algorithm and compared with CNN. SCG outperforms all classifiers with an accuracy of 95.8% and 82%. Furthermore, the relative outcomes indicate that the projected approach is more accurate than other methods of diagnosing skin cancer.

***Keywords:*** Segmentation, Classification, Preprocessing, Feature Extraction, Genetic Algorithm.

## Introduction

The relative incidence of skin lesions is growing at 3.1% per year. More than 3 million people in the US are diagnosed with skin lesions ([Shazia et al., 2016](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_1)). Therefore early detection of skin lesions is very important for the correct diagnosis of the disease. Malignant melanoma is of several subtypes. Basal cell and Squamous-cell carcinoma are the non-melanoma skin lesions forms. All kind of skin lesion has various characteristics from other types. The dermatologist utilizes an optical examination for the clinical perception of skin lesion identification. Objective characteristics become significantly worse than dermatoscopy and automated diagnosis.

Dermatoscopy is a non-intrusive symptomatic method. Few physicians use the ABCDE rule to modify characteristic performance ([Piccolo et al., 2014](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_2)). Consequently, there is a requisite for automatic diagnosis of melanoma from images. Now, the computerized technique is engaged by a decision support system, which aids the dermatologist to distinguish malignant melanoma from other types. The CAD system gives accurate results in less time ([Abbadi and Miry, 2014](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_3)). For a clinician to get accurate information regarding the lesion, automated skin lesion image processing provides improved outcomes. The four main stages in the automatic processing of skin lesions are Preprocessing, Lesion segmentation, Feature selection with extraction, and Lesion classification. The images are assimilated by a digital dermoscopy. Preprocessing is the mining of data from large datasets, and filtering it for further processing. In the pre-processing phase, the noise in the skin such as hairs and air bubbles is detached ([Arshaghi et al., 2020](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_4)). The filtering techniques used are Wiener, Gaussian, Image enhancement, and histogram equalization ([Chandrahasa et al., 2016](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_5)).

Segmentation is a crucial procedure for medical image processing applications and computer vision since the minute details of skin lesion needs to be considered. The process of partitioning an image into a component image is segmentation. This work used grayscale thresholding in K-Means, Otsu, edge detection, and histogram equalization method ([Abbas et al., 2013](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_6)). Identifying and extracting essential features in skin lesions is of utmost importance. Every skin lesion has various characteristics when compared to other types. Feature extraction abstracts information from lesion images ([Elgamal, 2013](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_7)). All pixels in the region have a resemblance of color, texture, and more. In the proposed work, the features of size, shape, color, texture, gray-level co-occurrence, and average energy are calculated for all the lesion images. Deep learning systems are extensively used for medical image analysis. For efficient extraction of features, the background image in the skin lesion is to be cast off.

The classification stage provides an interpretation of the mined information from the preceding phases to create an analysis regarding the lesion image. The grouping stage examines the benign from malignant skin lesions depending on the extricated features. Since the basic objective of feature selection lies in selecting the maximal features to execute high performance for skin lesion classification (Thaajwer and Ishanka, 2021 ). These extricated features certainly categorize the classes of skin cancer ([Nezhadian and Rashidi, 2018](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_9)). For the implementation, Training Scaled Conjugate Gradient (SGA) algorithm was engaged.

The current work consists of Section “Methodology” which summarizes the literature review. Section “Genetic Algorithm-based Feature Extraction” describes the methodology. Section “Implementation” provides an implementation of the proposed work and Section “Classification using a neural network with training Scale Conjugate Gradient Algorithm (SCGA)" describes lesion classification. Section “Conclusion” contains the conclusions.

## Literature Survey

Sheikh [Shazia et al. (2016](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_1)) developed a thermography method that uses temperature measurements to identify malignant lesions in the skin. The authors identified skin cancer as the most common type of carcinoma. An estimated 3 million Americans suffer from skin lesions. Melanoma is the deadliest of other types of skin cancer. The tools used are Image J 148 V.

Domenico [Piccolo et al. (2014](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_2)) carried out a dermoscopic analysis of Pigmented Skin Lesions (PSL) by the ABCD rule. The author concluded that for critical evaluation of the lesion, a small number of parameters are sufficient. 165 pigmented skin lesion images are considered and assessed by three dermatologists. The results proved to help improve diagnosis and are close to the medical practitioner’s assumption.

Nidhal Khdhair El Abbadi and Abbas Hussien Miry (2014) developed a CAD system for image segmentation. The Wiener filter was utilized for preprocessing and histogram thresholding segmentation. The proposed methods utilized Hammoude Distance (HD) and True Detection Rate (TDR). K-Means, Fuzzy C-Means, Otsu, Adaptive Threshold, Niblack, and Sovolas algorithmic segmentation techniques were used and the results were compared. The system achieved 96.32% accuracy.

Ali [Arshaghi et al. (2020](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_4)) proposed preprocessing by mean and Gaussian filters. Otsu partitioning technique for minimum error, maximum entropy, and fuzzy c mean was used. For feature selection, the color, shape, and a New Buzzard Optimization Algorithm (BUZO) with an accuracy of 94.3% were employed.

[Chandrahasa et al. (2016](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_5)) discussed skin cancer using smartphones. Various image processing approaches of grayscale conversion, histogram analysis, and border tracing are utilized. The paper concludes with feature extraction as the major pioneering skin lesion filtering system.

Qaiser [Abbas et al. (2013](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_6)) proposed a new unified method for automatic boundary detection (ABD). Otsu pre-processes using a normalized smoothing filter (NSF) with a mixture model (MM)

for segmentation to refine the lesion regions. 100 images from the EDRA Dermoscopy Interactive Atlas were considered. The acquired outcomes show that the ABD algorithm automatically finds skin lesion areas in dermatoscopic images. Additionally, a GUI is designed to demonstrate the ABD techniques.

Mahmoud [Elgamal (2013](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_7)) described a hybrid technique for feature extraction by DWT, dimensionality reduction using PCA, and classification. For classification, feed-forward backpropagation ANN and KNN are used. The two proposed classifiers provided an accuracy of 95% and 97.5% respectively.

[Ahmed Thaajwer and Piumi Ishanka (2021](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_8)) proposed a CAD for the initial diagnosis of melanoma. The image processing techniques of morphological and threshold segmentation methods are utilized. The color, shape, and GLCM of texture features are used with the SVM classifier. The author concluded that the features are combined to achieve an accuracy of 83%.

Farzam Kharaji Nezhadian and Saeid Rashidi (2018) developed a new algorithm for skin cancer detection using active contour segmentation. The color and texture features are extracted for high efficacy with 97% accuracy using SVM for the ISIC dataset.

Mohamed Khaled Abu Mahmoud and Adel AI Jumaily (2014) analyzed the concept by image-resizing, image cropping, and filtering by Weiner, Gabor, and Adaptive median filter. The Edge detection-based method was employed which used SFS and 42 images of microscopic slides.

Ying Qian and Shuo Zhao (2020) developed CAD for the detection and identification of melanoma by Gaussian and Wiener filtering. The author suggested the projected work aims to choose the appropriate features for the ISIC dataset with 10.34% improved accuracy. The Otsu, color, and texture are employed. Multiple group discriminant correlation analysis (MDCA) was used to associate the traits.

Yoo Na [Hwang et al. (2021](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_12) ) developed a hybrid model merging rank set (HK-LS) and hierarchical k-means approach. PH² and Dermofit databases are considered. Pre-processing is performed by histogram equalization using a two-level joint segmentation model based on the DRLSE model and fine boundary segmentation. The authors concluded that the proposed method showed good accuracy.

Prajakta Sanjay Gaikwad et al. (2013) discussed SVM using color space conversion, and feature extraction by shape, color, and texture. The shape features considered are image diameter, compactness, ulnar variance, and asymmetry. And the coarseness and GLCM for texture features are calculated. Variance, skewness, and entropy are evaluated for the color features. The K-means provide an accuracy of 52.63% and an SVM of 80 to 90%.

Ritesh [Maurya et al. (2014](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_15)) designed GLCM-based texture features as input to Multi-class SVM for classification. The author classified the given dataset into tetrad classes with 81.43% accuracy using Matlab 7.12. The GLCM feature uses the autocorrelation of entropy energy variance and uniformity.

Walid [Barhoumi et al. (2007](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_16)) discussed Computer-Aided Diagnostic (CAD) system for skin lesion malignancy grounded on lesion description and decision. The Content- Based-Image-Retrieval (CBIR) schemes were utilized. The lesion malignancy was detected by the Dempster-Shafer theory to improve the accuracy by 89%. The dull razor filter was applied and 21 features for shape and radiometric properties were calculated.

Lisheng [Wei et al. (2018](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_17)) discussed skin cancer identification with feature discernment grounded on fine-grained classification principles with U-Net architecture and migration testing strategy. The author concluded that the outcome indicated better performance for ISBI 2016 dataset.

Yanhui [Guo et al. (2018](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_18)) proposed an innovative neutrosophic clustering based on an adaptive region-growing algorithm by NCARG for skin detection. The images employed Shearlet transform. The dataset employs 500 images for the dataset preparation. The projected system attained 95.3% accuracy.

Julie Ann et al. (2018) developed deep learning to detect melanoma automatically for the PH² dataset. The morphological operation of erosion and dilation is utilized and AlexNet is for the pre-trained network. Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with Step Gradient Momentum (SGDM) is used for network training which attained an accuracy of 93% with 86% to 94% of sensitivity and specificity.

## Methodology

The proposed framework employs automatic skin lesion detection. [Figure 1](#ch2.xhtml#fig2_1) describes the projected framework.

[Fig. 1\. An outline schematic of the projected framework](#ch2.xhtml#R_fig2_1)

## Image Preprocessing

The images are acquired and cropped, converted to grayscale images ([Mahmoud and Jumaily, 2014](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_10)). The filtering methods of Wiener and Gaussian are employed here. Weiner filters are used to restore a blurry skin lesion image ([Qian and Zhao, 2020](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_11)). A pixel-wise adaptive approach is centered on the local neighborhood of arbitrary dimensions of every pixel. To control the extent of blurring, a Gaussian filter is used. For an enhanced feature image, the lesion images are resized by contrast enhancement. The original and cropped (resized) images for dataset 1 in frame 1 are shown in [Figs. 2a and b](#ch2.xhtml#fig2_2). To enhance the contrast of the image, histogram equalization is implemented.

![Fig. 2. (a) Original Image (b)Resized Image in framel for datasetl](images/fig2_2_C.jpg)

[Fig. 2\. (a) Original Image (b)Resized Image in framel for datasetl](#ch2.xhtml#R_fig2_2)

## Segmentation

In medical imaging, segmentation denotes segregating skin lesions into different fragments in which each fragment corresponds to different naturally significant structures. The segmentation techniques of threshold, edge detection, K-Means, Otsu, gray level thresh, and histogram equalization are carried out in this work.

The grayscale imagery is taken as input for adaptive thresholding which outputs a binary image. The Global method of gray level thresh is calculated in which a single pixel is used for all levels. The edge detection methods like Roberts, Sobel, Prewitt, Canny, and Log were used. From the output of the edge detection, Canny gives better results as in [Fig. 3](#ch2.xhtml#fig2_3). A Centroid-based K-means clustering algorithm is used ([Hwang et al., 2021](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_12)). Here each group is characterized by a vector and objects are allocated to a cluster centered on squared distance. A global adaptive binarization Otsu segmentation that separates foreground and background images is cast off. From the segmentation implementation, the threshold grounded segmentation of the malignant ISIC\_0025234 image gives improved quality and precise lesion segmentation as in [Fig. 4](#ch2.xhtml#fig2_4). For the next phase of the work, the histogram equalized image for dataset 1 in frame 1 is measured as input to feature selection as in [Fig. 5](#ch2.xhtml#fig2_5).

## Adaptive Genetic Algorithm-based Feature Extraction

Identifying the most effective feature is a crucial part of skin lesion detection. For the proposed datasets 1 and 2, the features of size, image contrast, color, texture, Gray Level Cooccurrence Matrix (GLCM), average energy, and shape are estimated ([Gaikwad et al., 2021](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_13); [Maurya et al., 2014](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_15); [Barhoumi et al., 2007](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_16)). A total of 26 attributes are estimated from these features. A comparison of the features from the literature survey papers is presented in [Table 1](#ch2.xhtml#tab2_1). The algorithm for feature extraction is as shown.

[Table 1\. A comparison of feature extraction](#ch2.xhtml#R_tab2_1)

  
| References || Feature Extraction - Features |
| --- | --- |
| \[[9](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_9)\] \[H\] \[[13](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_13)\] || Color and texture |
| --- | --- |
| \[[3](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_3)\] || Contrast enhancement |
| \[[14](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_14)\] || GLCM |
| \[[7](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_7)\] || DWT, PCA |
| \[[6](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_6)\] \[[12](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_12)\] || Shape |

Genetic Algorithm-based Feature Extraction

Step 1: Scan the imagery

### \# Size feature

Step 2: Rescale the imagery

Step 3: Modify the imagery to a grayscale Step 4: Compute SI and S2 as the minimum and maximum value

Step 5: Convert the image to histogram equalized image

### \# Image contrast

Step 6: Calculate image contrast as the difference between the maximum and minimum of a grayscale value

### \# Color feature

Step 7: Compute the maximum and mean value of Red, Green, and Blue colors in an image

### \# Texture feature

Step 8: Using the grayscale image, calculate the mean (1^(st) moment) and standard deviation (2^(nd) moment)

Step 9: Select a window size

For every pel (i, j) in the imagery:

1.  Center the window at pixel (i, j)
2.  Compute the texture feature Skew (3^(rd) moment) and Kurtosis (4^(th) moment)

© The computed value is distributed to the center pixel (i, j) in a new image

### \# Gray Level Co-occurrence Matrix

Step 10: Convert histogram equalized image to grayscale

Step 11: Compute the graycomatrix of the image to get the normalized values

Step 12: The values are computed for Gl by dividing the graycomatrix by the maximum value of graycomatrix

Step 13: The position of Gl is utilized for the GA selection operation. Assign it as G-High. (If G1==1)

### \# GLCM Feature

Step 14: Compute energy (intensity variation), entropy (gray level distribution)

Step 15: Evaluate the contrast of the image as a measure of intensity and homogeneity.

### \# Fourier Transform

Step 16: Based on the mutation operator of the genetic algorithm, the values are chosen based on the AC coefficient.

Step 17: Average energy is calculated based on the mask

### \# Shape Feature

Step 18: For each pixel (i, j) in the image:

1.  Calculate the ROI of the boundary
2.  Compute Compactness, perimeter, Eccentricity, Convex Hull Area, and Mass Deficient Coefficient (MDC)
3.  The AC energy and MDC are saved for the future (Elitism).

### Dataset preparation

For this work, the images are acquired from the ISIC Archive dataset. Two datasets are proposed. Dataset-1 includes a total of 98 images and dataset-2 contains 100 images. Both datasets contain images of benign and malignant from ISIC archive MSK-1, MSK-2, UDA-1, UDA-2, and HAM10000. [Table (2)](#ch2.xhtml#tab2_2) describes the dataset. ## Result Analysis

Resized images of histogram equalization are fed as input to segmentation. The segmented output is feature extracted based on size, image contrast, color, texture, GLCM, average energy, and shape respectively. Hence seven features are identified to be significant in detecting lesions.

Our experimental results show better performance compared to other methods ([Wei et al., 2018](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_17); [Guo et al, 2018](#ch2.xhtml#ref2_18); Ann et al., 2018). The computation overhead is reduced by using the SCGA algorithm. The accuracy of various datasets with the classifier used is depicted in [Table 3](#ch2.xhtml#tab2_3). ## Classification Using a Neural Network with Training Scale Conjugate Gradient Algorithm (SCGA)

This work implements a training Scaled Conjugate Gradient Algorithm (SCGA) for effective skin lesion categorization. SCGA belongs to the category of a supervised learning algorithm. From the proposed datasets 1 and 2, 25 features are considered. The proposed dataset 1 and 2 includes 98 and 100 instances respectively, for 2 classes benign (Class 0) and malignant (Class 1). The classification outcome of both datasets is shown in [Table 4](#ch2.xhtml#tab2_4).

## Conclusion

The projected system is utilized for the automatic melanoma skin lesions diagnosis employing an image processing approach and trained with a Scaled Conjugate Gradient Algorithm (SCGA). The system uses a proposed database to classify skin lesions. A total of 26 attributes are evaluated in feature extraction and fed for classifier training. The accuracy of the current system is improved by concentrating on the features. The accuracy obtained from the SCGA classifier is 95.8% and 82% for datasets 1 and 2. The error rate for Proposed Data Set 1 is 0.0417 and 0.1800 for Proposed Data Set 2. From the classification results of the proposed data set 1 and proposed data set 2, the system achieved good accuracy.

# Trust Aware Energy Efficient Model Using Evolutionary Computing in WSN

Mythili Varatharajan,^([²](#fn2))

DOI: [10.1201/9781003430452-3](https://dx.doi.org/10.1201/9781003430452-3)

## Abstract

In recent times, the centralized network management and control in Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs) is brought by Software-Defined Networking (SDN). Such flexible management and control using SDN offer two major solutions to energy and security, which have been treated as critical issues. With such motivation, the study develops a model that integrates direct-, indirect-, and mutual trust between the sensor nodes to mitigate the forwarding attacks including new-flow and selective forwarding attacks. All the three-trust value is sent as a distributed input to the trust management evolutionary controller that evaluates the attacks at the node level. The reduction in trust level tends to discard the node and label it as malicious and vice versa. Further, the computational requirements are handled in an efficient manner, where the data packets are aggregated and forwarded to avoid energy consumption. The simulation results show that the proposed method achieves higher energy consumption and trust level than the other existing methods.

***Keywords:*** Wireless Sensor Networks, Software-Defined Networking, trust value, forwarding attacks

## Introduction

As the capabilities of sensors have improved, battery-operated wireless sensor networks (WSNs) have found their way into many different types of industrial settings ([Liu et al., 2022](#ch3.xhtml#ref3_1); [Gite et al., 2021](#ch3.xhtml#ref3_2)). Vehicle traffic monitoring is just one example; other uses include the Internet of Things (IoT), smart industries, and public safety networks. In addition to their use in fields like environmental monitoring, vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) communication, and healthcare, wireless sensor networks (WSNs) have many more practical uses ([Singh et al., 2022](#ch3.xhtml#ref3_3); [Yadav and Kumar 2022](#ch3.xhtml#ref3_4)).

The nodes, or sensors, in a WSN communicate with one another via radio waves but are otherwise autonomous. The network is secured by a central base station (BS). These nodes can exchange information with one another and their surroundings by keeping tabs on the state of several physical parameters. The BS responsibility is to gather data from various sources, process it, and deliver it to the user so that the user may make informed decisions ([Maheswari and Karthika, 2021](#ch3.xhtml#ref3_5)). WSN nodes rely entirely on their internal, non-replaceable batteries. Furthermore, storage, memory, and CPU processing capabilities are constrained on sensor nodes ([Singh and Khare, 2021](#ch3.xhtml#ref3_6)).

It is essential to employ energy-efficient routing algorithms to extend the life of the network ([Rezvi et al., 2021](#ch3.xhtml#ref3_7)). As packets go from sensor nodes to the BS, radio waves play a role. More power is required to send information directly to the BS rather than in phases over shorter distances. Most studies have focused on clustering, wherein all members of the cluster have direct contact with the cluster central coordinator (CH). After that, the CH sends its combined, compressed data to the BS or a nearby CH ([Kaur and Rattan, 2021](#ch3.xhtml#ref3_8)).

Data compression, the elimination of unnecessary data, and the transmission of data across several hops are all made possible through clustering. Clustering useful outcomes are dependent on the accuracy of the approach taken and the viability of the parameters used. In contrast to distributed clustering algorithms, which are executed by individual sensor nodes utilizing location-specific data, centralized clustering algorithms are executed by the BS ([Jin 2021](#ch3.xhtml#ref3_9)). The goal is to find the best possible clustering solutions, so this is done.

Maintaining a secure network could be difficult due to various issues. Credible data gathering is a vital part of every study. Establishing and maintaining trust is crucial in many settings, including the military. Several algorithms for choosing a CH for WSNs don’t factor in security. Almost all modern security-aware protocols rely on cryptographic technologies, yet this is insufficient when facing enormous challenges. The use of cryptography increases network complexity, creates unnecessary extra effort, and slows it down. Therefore, it is important to think of a method of WSN security that is straightforward and uses little of the available resources ([Singh et al., 2022](#ch3.xhtml#ref3_3)).

In present work, we use Cuckoo Search algorithm to formulate the CH selection. This algorithm employs the ideas of population subdivision and subsequent generations. Cauchy-based exploration operations are a welcome addition to the algorithm because they support CS natural exploratory set. Here we propose a novel clustering approach, which combines the Cuckoo Search (CS) ([Cuong-Le et al., 2021](#ch3.xhtml#ref3_11)). Algorithm and trust estimations to choose CHs. The Cuckoo Search Algorithm is the name given to this process. The CS algorithm has been recognized as a viable option in the field of optimization research from its initial presentation. To prove its worth and get closer to the position of a standard benchmark, the CS algorithm has been subjected to extensive modification.

With such motivation, the study develops a model that integrates direct-, indirect-, and mutual trust between the sensor nodes to mitigate the forwarding attacks including new-flow and selective forwarding attacks. All the three-trust value is sent as a distributed input to the trust management evolutionary controller that evaluates the attacks at the node level. The reduction in trust level tends to discard the node and label it as malicious and vice versa.

## Related works

To extend the lifetime of wireless sensor networks (WSNs), many solutions have been applied. These include mobile relays, optimal positioning of sensor nodes, and energy harvesting. The LEACH protocol has been at the forefront of efforts to reduce network power consumption through routing and clustering ([Heinzelman et al., 2000](#ch3.xhtml#ref3_12)). This protocol employs a hierarchical clustering-based routing technique. This strategy generates multiple distinct clusters, each of which has its own CH. The data sent by the member nodes of each group is received by the CH node, which subsequently forwards the combined data to the BS.

There are protocols based on hierarchical clustering that involve more than one hop, in addition to the single-hop protocols that are the most common. Data can move in either direction using PEGASIS networks, which are formed by connecting chains of sensor nodes ([Lindsey and Raghavendra, 2002](#ch3.xhtml#ref3_13)). HEED chooses the CH node based on its proximity to other nodes in the network and the total amount of energy available at the time of the decision ([Younis and Fahmy, 2004](#ch3.xhtml#ref3_14)). Multi-hop routing is used to transmit data between clusters in the energy-efficient uneven clustering (EEUC) protocol, which divides the network of sensor nodes into clusters of varying sizes. The purpose of this protocol is to lessen the load on the CH node nearest to the BS in terms of energy usage ([Li et al., 2005](#ch3.xhtml#ref3_15)).

Many alternative variants of the LEACH protocol have been developed, all with the same goal in mind: to lessen the energy consumption of a network. In LEACH-C ([Heinzelman et al., 2002](#ch3.xhtml#ref3_16)), one coordinator runs and makes sure each cluster is assembled properly. The centralized coordinator of the necessary network data and providing it as a service to the optimized clusters. For instance, in LEACH-CE ([Tripathi et al, 2013](#ch3.xhtml#ref3_17)), a CH selection has been enhanced. The CH node is typically the cluster node with the most retained energy. Because of this, the network can handle the combined energy consumption of all the nodes. LEACH-CKM ([Mechta et al, 2014](#ch3.xhtml#ref3_18)) uses a K-means (or K-medians) clustering algorithm to improve the efficiency of the clustering procedure. If you use an energy-efficient smart building technique, your network will last much longer.

Based on their approach to data collection, sensor networks can be divided into two categories: proactive and reactive, as described by [Manjeshwar and Agrawal (2001](#ch3.xhtml#ref3_19)). In the reactive mode, nodes update key parameters in real time, while in the proactive mode, sensors respond at regular intervals. The detected data will not be sent to the base station until an event occurs that meets both the soft and hard thresholds (BS). TEEN is a reactive routing approach that can help cut down on transmissions that aren’t essential or are sent twice. When compared to the standard WSN protocols in use today, TEEN provides dramatically better energy efficiency. The APTEEN extension to TEEN developed by [Manjeshwar et al. (2002](#ch3.xhtml#ref3_20)) is well adapted to both the delivery of routine information and the management of emergencies.

Enhanced-SEP (E-SEP) ([Aderohunmu and Deng, 2009](#ch3.xhtml#ref3_21)) was developed to replace the SEP ([Smaragdakis et al., 2004](#ch3.xhtml#ref3_22)) two-tiered hierarchy with a new, more efficient three-tiered one. In E-SEP, sensors are divided into a high-end tier and a standard tier, with the high-end tier having access to significantly more energy than the standard tier.

[Kang and Nguyen (2012](#ch3.xhtml#ref3_23)), LEACH distance thresholds were originally their aim. The LEACH-DT algorithm considers the CH distance from the BS while calculating its selection probability. These separations are considered variables. BS calculates the distance between every pair of nodes and the probability function for the network. The BS then sends this data to every node in the network. Without a governing body, sensors still utilize the following data to choose which CH to employ. Multi-hop routing was also recommended by LEACH-DT, with the nodes being divided into subgroups according to their distance from the BS. Data transmission power can be drastically cut with multi-hop transmission because the information is moved from more distant nodes to those closer to the source.

Because of their use of weighted metrics, Cluster Chain-Weighted Metrics (CCWM) ([Mahajan et al., 2014](#ch3.xhtml#ref3_24)) can boost network performance while also reducing energy consumption. A set of CHs have been chosen for further study based on these criteria. With the help of ad hoc communication, information can be sent from individual member nodes to the CHs in charge of those nodes. The selected CHs will be used to build a routing chain that will allow for inter-cluster communication. Each CH in the line up to the BS will act as a relay, relaying data to the next CH in line. There is additional network overhead associated with reselecting CH due to the inefficiency of the initial election of CH. Additionally, there is an inequity in energy use due to intra-cluster communication.

The SEECH protocol, first developed by [Tarhani et al. (2014](#ch3.xhtml#ref3_25)), is designed for use in recurrent data transfer scenarios. Individuals are responsible for choosing their own CHs and relay nodes in this system, which uses a decentralized process ([Tarhani et al., 2014](#ch3.xhtml#ref3_25)). To lessen the load on the CH power reserves, it is crucial to employ numerous types of relay nodes. When tested for its usefulness in massive WSNs, the SEECH protocol fared admirably.

To extend the network lifetime, Mittal et al. propose two reactive clustering techniques, DRESEP ([Mittal and Singh., 2015](#ch3.xhtml#ref3_26)) and SEECP (Mittal et al., 2017), in which CHs are selected on a periodic and deterministic basis, respectively. Both DRESEP and SEECP are named for these procedures.

## Extraction of Profile Attributes

To determine which profiles are malicious and which are legitimate, we first extract their unique identifiers. The profile attributes are broken down into two groups: general and attack models using an attack model ([Heinzelman et al., 2002](#ch3.xhtml#ref3_16)). Using profile identifying information, generic characteristics can be used to retrieve the profile qualities. This helps investigators tell the difference between a fake profile and a malicious one.

Because of the high dimensionality and sparseness of the rating matrix in a collaborative trust system, the shilling attack model is challenging to implement. Therefore, the attributed set (A) is extracted from the initial or attack profile using supervised detection methods. Because of this, the dataset dimensionality is reduced. In this hypothetical scenario, the profile attributes are extracted using the Eq. 1. In the proposed system, a *q*\-attribute extraction method is utilized.

It is either a real person profile or an attack profile, and the study knows which it is. However, we were willing to accept any user profile as real while testing.

## Optimization Problem Formulation

The purpose of using a cuckoo search experiment is to formulate a probability to find the malicious node in the network. Between the two node positions, there will always be a certain amount of range error. Here, the research focuses on finding the malicious node to minimize the probability of transmitting via malicious nodes.

We establish an objective function (Obj) as the Mean Square Error (MSE) between the real distance of estimated node coordinates and the estimated distance of true unknown node coordinates from the neighboring anchor nodes. Our estimates can be compared to our best guesses in this way. The *i*^(th) node (unknown) is located at (x, *y)*, while the *j*^(th) anchor node is located at *(x.*, y.) for this discussion. The object can be expressed as follows using Equation 2:

  
$$\\sigma\_{u} = \\left\\{ \\frac{\\Gamma(1 + \\lambda)\\sin\\left( \\frac{\\pi\\lambda}{2} \\right)}{\\Gamma\\Gamma\\frac{(1 + \\lambda)}{2}\\lambda^{\\frac{(\\lambda - 1)}{2}}} \\right\\}^{\\frac{1}{\\lambda}}$$

From our research, we conclude that the following equation should be used to adjust the step size:

  
$$\\alpha = \\alpha\_{\\max} - \\left( \\frac{N\_{i}}{N\_{u}} \\right)\\left( {\\alpha\_{\\max} - \\alpha\_{\\min}} \\right)$$

## Classification

Both the step size control factor *a* and the mutation probability *Pa* play a significant role in how well the CS algorithm can locate the optimal solution. When the parameters are fixed *Pa=*0.25 and α=0.01, the location accuracy decreases, which reduces the usefulness of WSN applications, and the convergence rate decreases, which reduces the lifespan of sensor nodes with limited energy resources due to the large number of iterations and long computational time. While many standard CS-based augmentation solutions have been given to accomplish certain goals, none of them have proven particularly useful for WSN localization. The goal of this study is, therefore, to provide a useful CS method for the localization of WSN nodes by drawing ideas from the factors.

The step size has seen one of the most dramatic changes. If the value is too small, as demonstrated by the Levy flight in equation (2), the search population will concentrate on a narrow band near the best answer for the local area found in the search that came before it. When it comes to developing novel approaches to exploring the whole breadth of the search space, the answer is the same. Finally, a global optimum solution cannot be found without doing a very large number of iterations, which could use a where

*α*max - maximum step size

*a*min - minimum step size;

*N[i] -* iteration number and

Nit - total iterations.

Equation 3 clearly shows that as the number of iterations increases, the step size *α* decreases. To facilitate a worldwide search, the step size is set to its utmost at the outset of the iterative procedure. The step size is then progressively shrunk to encourage local search. This modification is crucial because the population tends to converge toward a global optimal solution as the number of repetitions rises.

We use solution fitness to create a mutation probability, Pa, that can broaden the population’s genetic pool and prevent the population from collapsing into a small subset. Too high a mutation probability *Pa* prevents timely convergence acceleration, whereas too low a mutation probability *Pa* reduces accuracy and necessitates more iterations to get good performance. Therefore, make sure the value you specify for the Pa parameter is neither too high nor too low.

The mutation probability Pa is believed to be proportional to the value of an objective function, and hence the efficacy of the proposed solution. This claim is made using the industry-standard algorithm from the field of computer science.

A nest with a higher fitness value, that is, one that is closer to the current global optimum, stands a better chance of being included in the next generation population. On the other hand, the value of the mutation probability Pa will be significantly lower for a nest with a lower fitness value, which is further from the global optimum because such a nest has a greater chance of being discovered and replaced by a new random solution. An alternative way of expressing this is the chance of a different random solution.

The investigation above led to the following correction to the mutation probability *Pa:*

  
$$Pa(j) = \\begin{cases} {Pa\_{\\min} + \\left( {Pa\_{\\max} - Pa\_{\\min}} \\right) \\times K} & {K < 1} \\\\ \\frac{Pa\_{\\max}}{N\_{i}} & {j = 1,2,..,n} \\\\ \\end{cases}$$  

where *K=f(j)-f*[min], and this solely depends on the *j*^(th) solution quality; *f*(*j*) - fitness of *j*^(th) solution, *f*min - global optimal fitness, *P*[max] - maximum mutation probability, *P*[min] - minimum mutation probability.

The study uses the solution appropriateness, as shown in Equation, to modify Pa. If *K*≤1, then the *j*^(th) best solution will be nearly identical to the finest solution in the world right now. Some have argued that the quality of the current *j*^(th) solution, denoted by *K*, should be proportional to the mutation probability, denoted by *Pa.* When quality improves, the mutation probability, measured by the parameter *Pa*, decreases. If, however, *K* is greater than 1, the quality of the *j*^(th) solution is now far from the global ideal. Since the population will tend to move toward the global optimum as the number of iterations increases, we hypothesize that the mutation probability *Pa* will fluctuate in an unfavorable direction as the number of iterations increases.

Additionally, the population is confined to a certain area, preventing any exploration, and thus saving energy. That is, we substitute the extremes of the range for solutions that are outside of it. We present an improved version of the CS method that finds the global optimum quickly and precisely by accounting for these and other considerations. ## Results and Discussions

Network Intrusion Detection (NID) (intrusion-detection) dataset is being utilized to perform a cost-benefit analysis for the current investigation. The system relies on Matlab, which is installed on a PC with 16 GB of RAM, Windows 7, and an Intel Core i7 processor. For each TCP/IP connection, 41 quantitative and qualitative features are obtained from normal and DDoS attack data (3 qualitative and 38 quantitative features).

## Evaluation metrics

Measures like recall and false positives can be used to assess the effectiveness of the proposed system.

**Recall:** The recall of a system is the number of attacks that were successfully uncovered by it.

  
$$\\text{~Recall~} = \\frac{TP}{TP + FN}$$  

**Precision:** The overall number of detected profiles in the system to the number of attack profiles discovered provides insight into the trust system accuracy.

  
$$\\text{~Precision~} = \\frac{TP}{TP + FN}$$  

**False positive Rate:** The false positive rate of a recommendation system is defined as the number of false positives produced in comparison to the total number of attack profiles.

  
$$FPR = \\frac{FP}{TP}$$

One strategy to evaluate CS with various direct, indirect, and mutual trust is to utilize varying attack sizes in conjunction with different detection strategies. Classifiers such as direct, indirect, and mutual trust for shilling detection methods are utilised to assess the effectiveness of the proposed approach. Evaluations are performed, and the outcomes are compared. Here, we’ll observe what happens when we increase the attack size from 1% to 2% to 5% to 10% to 20% while keeping the attack size constant at 3%. In addition to the attack model, the proposed technique is tested for its resilience against DDoS. [Tables 2](#ch3.xhtml#tab3_2) and 3 show the outcomes of the various detection attempts.

Both CS and the recommended strategy have improved recall as attack size grows. In addition, the proposed technique has a higher recall rate than CS and other methods, although the recall rates of the push and nuke attacks are quite low and show little to no differences between them. When the attack size is reduced to 10%, the proposed method achieves a success rate that is far closer to 100% than any other method. This shows that the proposed approach generates few false positives.

## Conclusions

To achieve this goal, the study builds a model that incorporates direct-, indirect-, and mutual trust between the sensor nodes, hence protecting against forwarding attacks including new-flow and selective forwarding attacks. The trust management evolutionary controller, which assesses the malicious nodes, takes into account all three trust values as a centralized input. Energy efficiency is obtained when the packet transmission occurs based on the trust between the nodes and transmission is not carried out via these malicious nodes in this research. If other nodes stop trusting a node, that node has a higher risk of being labeled as malicious, and vice versa. Further, data packets are bundled together and sent onward to reduce energy use while still satisfying processing needs. The simulation results show that the proposed strategy not only reduces energy consumption but also improves reliability in comparison to conventional approaches.

# Introspection of CNN Primitive Features for Indian Sign Language Based Hand Gesture Recognition of Daily Used Words Using Machine Learning

S. Gnanapriya^([³](#fn3))

E-mail: (phone: 91+ 9841799718; [gnanapriya.sl6@gmail.com](mailto:gnanapriya.sl6@gmail.com))

DOI: [10.1201/9781003430452-4](https://dx.doi.org/10.1201/9781003430452-4)

## Abstract

The recognition of Indian Sign Language (ISL) based daily used words, enables people who are unable to hear and speak to communicate with normal society to express their daily needs without the involvement of human translators. Though research on hand gesture recognition(HGR) has been in vogue for the past two decades, the recently popular Human-computer interaction (HCl) systems for hand gesture recognition use deep learning, which requires a high-specification system and hardware. The proposed novel system extracts 3 frames per second from the shown input gesture and addresses the changes in the lighting conditions of the image and uses unsupervised transfer learning to extract gesture features from the initial layer of the pre-trained Convolutional Neural Network ( CNN). Since the extracted two-dimensional matrices of features are too huge to handle, the machine learning-based dimensionality reduction technique Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) is used to automatically lessen the dimension of the feature vectors of each frame, by generating a unique gesture subspace for each gesture class and storing it in a database. The K-Nearest Neighbor distance measure is used for classification. Except for a few dynamic gestures the system recognized all the other gestures with high accuracy and the performance is on par with the existing methods at less resource cost and training time.

***Keywords:*** ISL, HCI, HGR, CNN, Feature vector, SVD, Dimensionality reduction, Deep Learning, Machine Learning, Transfer Learning

Subject classification codes: Image Processing, Machine Learning, Deep Learning

## Introduction

Hand Gesture seems to be a great medium of communication for hearing and mute disabled persons in the normal world, as well as for Human-Computer and Human-Robot Interaction (HRI). The ISL hand signs could be shown using one hand ([Fallucchi and Zanzotto, 2009](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_10)) or two hands (Mammen et al. 2015) which are of the static or dynamic type (Danilo [Avola et al. 2019](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_8); [Li et al. 2020](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_14)). The change in illumination is handled by [Fallucchi and Zanzotto (2009](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_10)) by converting the image to YCbCr space and the feature extraction by Discrete wavelet transform(DWT) and F-ratio tested against ASL dataset. The complex static hand gesture is handled by [Fallucchi and Zanzotto (2009](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_10)) with the help of a black color wristband on both hands for feature extraction, and the watershed algorithm and region merging techniques are used for segmentation. The gesture exposed could correspond to the words and sentences ([Li et al. 2020](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_14)) or finger spelling ([Mammen et al. 2015](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_15)). The recurrent Neural Network model LSTM is used to identify hand signs corresponding to words and sentences by splitting the continuous signs into sub-parts; these sub-parts are used to train the model. The knowledge gained by the network of sub-units is used to identify the dynamic gestures corresponding to words and sentences. The static image (Donq-Liang [Lee et al. 2018](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_9)) could be an RGB image ([Gnanapriya and Rahimunnisa, 2022](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_12)) taken using hand-held cameras, 3D images captured using a stereo camera, Kinect depth image (Donq-Liang [Lee et al. 2018](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_9); [Gnanapriya and Rahimunnisa, 2022](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_12); [Pan and Yang, 2010](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_23)) or skeletal image, hand data points generated by leap motion controller ([Li et al. 2020](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_14)) using IR cameras or IR diodes, whereas the ([Li et al. 2019](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_11)) tracks the fingertip using dense optical flow and skin filter to recognize the dynamic gestures. [Li et al. (2020](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_14)) used a leap motion controller that uses IR camera and IR diodes to emit IR light corresponding to finger bone joints, palm center, and wrist at the rate of 120 frames per second to recognize the hand gesture. Donq-Liang [Lee et al. (2018](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_9)) used a Microsoft Kinect camera to capture the RGB color image and depth image of the gesture. This overcomes the change in the lighting condition of the image and image with a complex background; feature extraction and recognition are carried out with the CNN. In literature to recognize hand gestures, various Image processing (Donq-Liang [Lee et al. 2018](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_9)), machine learning (Danilo [Avola et al. 2019](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_8); Donq-Liang [Lee et al, 2018](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_9)), computer vision (Donq-Liang [Lee et al. 2018](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_9)) and Deep learning (Wu et al. 2016) techniques or the combination of these approaches that use either the model-based approach (Danilo [Avola et al. 2019](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_8); Sahoo, 2018) or appearance based approach (Donq-Liang [Lee et al. 2018](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_9); [Fallucchi and Zanzotto, 2009](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_10); [Li et al. 2019](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_11); [Gnanapriya and Rahimunnisa, 2022](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_12)) are used. With the recent progression in Machine learning and Deep learning techniques, the recognition accuracy has reached the maximum, but at the expense of more time and resources. The proposed approach aims to provide accuracy almost equal to that of Deep learning at no additional time or resources by using Transfer Learning. Transfer learning avoids labeling and provides a new learning framework. Unsupervised Transfer Learning does not have either target domain labels or source domain labels an additional advantage. The decrease in the disparity between the source and target domains lowers classification error ([Singha and Laskar, 2015](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_18)).

## Related Work

Hand sign was the only medium of communication for the deaf and mute society. In a country like India where we have a diverse population, communicating with people of neighboring states itself is challenging, as the misinterpretation of daily used words may lead to miscommunication; to overcome this issue various research works have been carried out during the last few decades using vision based and sensor-based techniques. Vision-based technique is more appropriate for real-time processing as it does not require any laboratory setup. The hand gesture recognition system finds wide applications in the field of HCl, HRI, gaming, and ambient assisted living of an elderly person, with a driverless car. The gestures for human and Humanoid Robot Interaction impart an interaction between human and humanoid robots using image processing. The simulation was done using WEBOTS simulation software and tested against the HOAP-2 robot ([Nandy et al. 2010](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_4)). The authors ([Sharma and Anand, 2020](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_22)) consider hand trajectory to recognize the shown gestures from dynamic input. Hand Gesture Recognition(HGR) from the depth image captured using a Kinect camera improves the communication between humans and machines by understanding human behavior. The paper ([Wadhawan and Kumar, 2020](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_2)) detects the fingertip and follows the fingertip trajectory to extract geometrical features of fingers like length, width, and orientation of the finger to determine the hand gesture. The extracted geometrical features corresponding to the shown gesture are stored in a unique gesture subspace using SVD. The Grassmann manifold-based discriminant analysis is used to analyze the dependent variable used for recognizing the test gesture. This sentence is not clear. [Bommert et al. (2020](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_1)) used CNN for feature extraction from a Kinect depth image and SVM for classification. It addresses the changes in light variation and background variation. The CNN extracts local spatial patterns and temporal dynamics of motion from successive semantic video frames. The Vector of pooled semantic video clips forms the vector subspace called Grassmann match kernels (GMK). The canonical correlations are used to match the videos for action recognition ([Nandy et al. 2010](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_4)). A survey of statistical dimensionality reduction methods. [Verma and Choudhary (2020](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_6)) are used to handle high dimensional data as it has more redundant information, it is removed without significant loss of information using mathematical procedures like statics or Machine learning with mathematical insight behind it. Dimensionality reduction reduces the complexity of data structures and maintains the information. Feature selection is an emerging problem in recent trends due to the increase in higher dimensionality data. Filter methods select relevant features and reduce the run time and improve the prediction accuracy of machine learning algorithms ([Mittal et al. 2019](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_3)). The Indian Sign Language gesture includes static and dynamic signs which are one or two-handed. The purpose of the video database is to keep several videos for numerous signs. To combat changes in illumination and direction, the Direction Histogram is used. The recognition of the shown gesture is carried out using distance measures like Euclidean distance and K-nearest neighbor metrics ([Sorzano and Vargas, 2014](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_7)). The pre-trained model or a portion of it can be used to extract the features. The continuous gesture sequence corresponding to words and sentences is determined by [Li et al. (2020](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_14)) using the RNN architecture LSTM. The input to the system is IR light generated from 12 data points corresponding to ten fingertips and two palm centers by the leap motion controller. It divides the continuous gesture into subunits and trains the system with these subunits. The gestures corresponding to the words and sentences that use the trained sub units are recognized by the predictive model. Hand gestures play a major role in human-computer interaction. As the feature vector corresponding to a hand sign changes over time RNN is used (Sahoo, 2018). The feature points given by the leap motion controller, the intra-finger angles, and the angles formed between finger phalanges determine the gesture. [Sinha et al. (2019](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_20)) generate fused gesture data using the spatial fuzzy matching algorithm that fuses spatial information from the leap motion controller to construct a dataset. [Zhang et al. (2018](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_21)) address the interesting challenge called self-occlusion of gesture during the segmentation stage. The neural network classifier was trained to utilize innovative features such as the distance from the palm center and, the number of self-co-articulated strokes, direction of the hand, the distance between start and end points, and the number of self-co-articulated strokes, which are found to be effective at spotting gestures.

The proposed approach handles changes in the lighting conditions in the image and applies transfer learning to minimize the training time. The novelty of the proposed system resides in extracting the first hidden layer feature vector of the input frames. The frame rate of 3 frames per second corresponding to the shown gesture is considered for processing. As CNN generates a huge volume of features, Singular value decomposition, a Machine learning based dimensionality reduction technique is used to manage the extracted features. The selective feature vectors reduce the processing time and run on systems with normal specifications.

## Proposed System

The advantage of CNN is its perception which is almost equal to that of humans but at the cost of a high-performance computing system and GPU. The proposed system uses the unsupervised pre-trained Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) VGG-16 as it increases the learning rate of the target predictive model using the gained knowledge.

Supervised Transfer Learning transfers the gained knowledge from the source domain to improve the target predictive model when their domain and task are similar, and both the source model and target model have labeled data ([Singha and Laskar, 2015](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_18)).

The novelty of the proposed work resides in extracting the first hidden layer output as a feature vector for any shown gesture input. Training a neural network is time and resource-consuming. The pre-trained VGG16 model downloads the weight file, for convolution is redefined to output after the first hidden layer. The architecture of the proposed method is shown in [Fig. 1](#ch4.xhtml#fig4_1) and the model summary is shown in [Fig. 2](#ch4.xhtml#fig4_2). The obtained feature map is shown in [Fig. 3](#ch4.xhtml#fig4_3) and the corresponding feature maps visualization is shown in [Fig. 4](#ch4.xhtml#fig4_4). From [Fig. 3](#ch4.xhtml#fig4_3) it is apparent that transformation from a high dimensional space to a low dimensional space is required and this is achieved using an unsupervised way of feature selection using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) ([Gangrade and Bharti, 2020](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_17)). The dataset consists of both static and dynamic gestures, as shown in [Table 2](#ch4.xhtml#tab4_2). The feature vectors of the three input frames of the corresponding gesture are taken at the rate of 3 frames /per second and given as input to SVD. The average of three SVD approximated values is computed, as shown in [Fig. 5](#ch4.xhtml#fig4_5) and stored in the database as shown in [Table 2](#ch4.xhtml#tab4_2). The advantage of SVD is, it automatically performs dimensionality reduction as the data is sparse, by projecting the dataset and selecting the principal component of projection.

## Preprocessing and Feature extraction using VGG-16

VGG-16, the pre-trained ImageNet model for Keras is a 16-layered Deep Convolutional Neural Network for Large-Scale Image Recognition and used for feature extraction. The model handles changes in the lighting condition of the image as color normalization is carried out, using mean RGB subtraction during preprocessing. The proposed work extracts feature from the output of the first hidden layer of a 16-layer deep network. The network uses receptive fields of size 3x3 weight matrix that has been convolved over the image using the stride of one and ReLu activation function. The model uses Max pooling of size 2x2, and zero padding of size lxl to preserve the spatial resolution after convolution ([Simonyan and Zisserman, 2015](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_19)).

The pre-trained unsupervised transfer learning model does not use labeled data in both the source and target domains. It supports the input image of size 224x224 and automatically takes the weight as ImageNet from Keras. Unsupervised Transfer Learning transfers the gained knowledge from source domain to improve the target predictive model when their domain and task are similar, while source learns from labeled data and the target model has unlabeled data ([Singha and Laskar, 2015](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_18)).

## Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)

The number of feature maps produced for the input image is directionally proportional to the

size of the input image. Therefore, it is difficult to handle the generated huge volume of feature vectors; so an unsupervised feature selection method, the Singular value decomposition is used to reduce the dimension of the vector space.

The SVD of matrix M is

(1)  
*M* = *U*∑*V*^(*T*)  

where the size of the matrixes is

U →V^T → r x m, S → r x r. The diagonal elements of the matrix X are the singular values, such as δ ≥ δ2 ≥... ≥ δr> 0 where r is the rank of the matrix M. For the decomposition, SVD exploits the linear combination of rows and columns of M. The unsupervised ways of using SVD for feature reduction are interesting ways to exploit the approximated computations.

(2)  
*M* ≈ *M*[*k*] = *U*[*m* × *k*]∑[*k* × *k*]*V*[*k**x**n*]^(*T*)  

Where k is smaller than the rank r.

Given an SVD the pseudo-inverse matrix is

(3)  
*M*^+ = *V*∑*U*^(*T*)  

It is a natural feature selector. Iterative algorithms are used to calculate SVD. The dimensions that are originally derived have higher singular values. The k dimension is more informative than the k + 1; so it’s decided to have a single element as SVD approximation of the original matrix ([Gangrade and Bharti, 2020](#ch4.xhtml#ref4_17)). The obtained SVD approximations are unique for each class of gestures, so the distance measures stored in the database are used for classification.

## Classification using KNN

The database consists of the Gesture class. The normalized SVD approximation is created by running 30 samples under each class as shown in [Table 2](#ch4.xhtml#tab4_2). For dynamic gestures, the input images are collected at every 20 ms duration, which results in 3 samples per gesture. The feature vectors of these samples generated by the redefined CNN model are shrinking in dimension and averaged to compute the SVD approximation of the dynamic gesture, a sample of this is shown in [Fig. 5](#ch4.xhtml#fig4_5). The gesture recognition is done by finding the difference between the stored SVD approximations of Gesture classes with the obtained SVD for the given input gesture, using the K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN) distance measures. The gesture is classified by displaying the class label of the class that is closest to the taken input gesture.

## KNN steps

1.  the select K value, where k is the number of gestures close to the given input gesture to be found.
2.  Calculate the Euclidean distance between SVD approximation of Training input and all stored values.
    
      
    $$d(x,y) = \\sqrt{\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{m}{(x\_{i} - y\_{i})}^{2}}$$  
    
3.  Sort the obtained k distances in the ascending order
4.  Select the gesture which has a distance approximately equal to zero as the nearest neighbor.
5.  Make a prediction.

The one-handed gesture has fewer features compared to two-handed gestures. The types of gestures also play an important role in contributing to the feature vector. ## Conclusion

The pre-trained VGG-16 trained on an unsupervised Transfer learning setting speeds up feature extraction and improves the model performance using the weights of the previously trained model. The model eliminates the need for high-performance computing systems like GPU. The model also handles changes in the illumination conditions of the images. The obtained reduced SVD outputs best approximation to uniquely identify each gesture with high accuracy. Only the gestures arise, above and below which have spatial variation in the hand position with time. This is because each individual shows gestures with varying speeds based on their aging and physical fitness, or because the number of frames considered per second for calculating SVD approximation is only 3 frames/second. In the future, the change in spatial distance of such gestures could be taken into account, or taking more frames per second to achieve the best accuracy.
