# Surface Defect Detection for Wet Blue Leather Using Deep Learning Approach

Vinith Kumar^([^(31)](#fn31))

Department of Computer Science Engineering, Hindustan Institute of Technology and Science, Chennai, India

DOI: [10.1201/9781003430452-39](https://dx.doi.org/10.1201/9781003430452-39)

## Abstract

Due to the diverse nature of defects and the lack of publicly available data for algorithm benchmarking, automated visual inspection for leather defect detection is a challenging endeavor in the leather industry. The existing Leather Defect Detection methods are mostly done with manual inspection or during the later stage of the finished leather product. Traditional machine learning methods use hand-crafted features from the textural or transform domain, which takes a lot of computational time and it is hard to generalize. The proposed Leather Defect Detection method using Convolution Neural Network for blue wet leather identifies the defect in the earlier stage with 93.4% accuracy and lessens the processing cost and yields profit to the manufacturers. The IoT module in the proposed model sends the results of leather defect detection to the administrators and makes them monitor the process from a remote place by automating the defect detection process by reducing time and increasing the profit.

Keywords: Convolutional Neural Network, Data augmentation, Pre-trained models, Image processing, Computer vision, Blue wet leather

## Introduction

The leather industry is always looking for ways to cut costs while simultaneously increasing productivity and product quality. The detection of flaws in leather hides and skins is one crucial step toward achieving this objective. The time-consuming and error-prone process of manual inspection can clog the leather processing pipeline. Defect detection efficiency and accuracy can be enhanced by automated visual inspection systems, which can also reduce rejection costs. The convolutional neural networks (CNNs), focus on the detection of flaws in blue wet leather in this study. This procedure aids in the identification of flaws that may not be apparent in dry leather. The public dataset of blue wet leather images is used for transfer learning and data augmentation techniques to train and test the model.

## Stages in Leather processing:

1.  ***Pre-Treatment:*** The raw hides are prepared for processing at this stage.
2.  ***Tanning:*** The hides are treated with a tanning agent during the tanning process. Among the various kinds of tanning agents are mineral salts.
3.  ***Neutralization:*** The hides are treated with acid after they have been tanned to bring the pH level back to neutral and remove any excess tanning agent.
4.  ***Dyeing:*** the leather can be dyed to the desired color.
5.  ***Finishing:*** After that, the leather is finished to get the texture and appearance you want. Sanding, embossing, buffing.

## Challenges in the Leather Defect Detection:

There are a number of reasons why leather defect detection can be difficult, including:

1.  ***1.3 Leather quality variation:*** The quality of the leather can be significantly influenced by the raw materials’ origin, tanning method, and finishing techniques.
2.  ***1.4 The variety of leather’s patterns and textures:*** Defects in leather can be difficult to spot due to its sometimes-intricate patterns and textures.
3.  ***1.5 Individuality:*** Cowhide imperfection identification frequently includes visual assessment by human administrators.
4.  ***1.6 There is a limited supply of high-quality training data:*** High-quality labeled data are needed to train machine learning models for leather defect detection.

## Blue Wet Leather Stage:

Leather that has been tanned but has not yet been dried is known as “blue wet.” Due to the tanning process, the leather is still wet and has a bluish hue at this point. Tannins are added to hides or skins during the tanning process to stabilize and preserve them. The “blue wet” stage of leather processing is crucial because it’s when the leather is stretched and shaped to get the thickness, texture, and size you want.

The structure of the paper is as follows: In section 2, various use cases of deep learning are discussed, and in section 3, the related work on deep learning in leather defect detection is covered. Section 4 illustrates the existing leather detection. The proposed word on deep learning-based leather detection is presented in Section 4, and the conclusion is presented in Section 5.

## Use cases of Deep Learning

Neural networks with multiple layers are used in deep learning, a subset of machine learning, to solve complex problems. It has emerged as a crucial instrument in a number of fields, including:

***Recognizing images and videos:*** With high accuracy, deep learning models can recognize things, people, and activities in images and videos.

***Natural processing of language:*** In order to comprehend and generate human language, deep learning is utilized.

***Robotics:*** Robots can be taught to perform complex tasks like grasping objects, navigating environments, and interacting with humans using deep learning.

***Healthcare:*** Analyzing medical images, diagnosing diseases, and creating individualized treatment plans are all possible applications of deep learning.

## Related Work

In the existing leather detection system, to deal with voltage fluctuations brought on by an unstable power grid and speed changes brought on by transmission roller damage, Li Hongwei’s The Internet plus leather shotcrete machine system makes use of the Internet of Things’ CMT-SVR-200 technology, which features error-resistant transmission, double closed-loop speed regulation, and more (Jiyi et at., 2022). The shotcrete machine can precisely spray leather and simultaneously measure the leather as it goes through the photoelectric detection box. Customers will find it easier to inspect the goods as a result of this system.

The detriments of the ability to prepare in view of conventional businesses slowly become evident because of the quick progression of science and innovation. Universities’ efforts to cultivate talent face new challenges as a result of the profession’s slow growth, which frequently results in a lack of professional identity([Aslam et al., 2021](#ch39.xhtml#ref39_1)). The impact of the leather industry on information technology and the direction of higher education for leather professionals are examined. Automation’s expansion in the leather industry, automated leather defect classification has received a lot of attention. In recent years, numerous novel strategies to improve the automated defect classification pipeline have been presented (Mantari et at., 2022). The creation of new ideas is the primary objective of this study, as methods for the detection of leather defects, and the formulation of recommendations for the identification and selection of models.

A novel approach to resolving a number of tasks related to the labor market is provided by CNC machine control. To advocate for a technological solution for the hand-cut leather industry, maximize the collaborator’s safety, and reduce production time, this study demonstrates an endless screw motor control system for a CNC machine (Chen et at., 2021). The CNC machine’s cutting speed and duration in relation to the part’s size and shape were determined using simulated MATLAB software and a variety of parameters in the project.

One of the processes is sorting crust leather from various animal species used to sort leather. This procedure is typically carried out by hand and takes a significant amount of time by a group of experts ([Vasagam et al., 2022](#ch39.xhtml#ref39_7)). Consequently, the authors created INT\_LEA\_IMG\_CLRI\_UNOM, a brand-new dataset consisting of 609 images from the Training and Testing datasets. The LAPLACIAN, MEDIAN, SOBEL, ROBERTS, SCHARR, PREWITT, and GAUSSIAN pre-processing filters and Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLARE) are used to improve the images. The proposed approach’s classification accuracy is significantly confirmed by employing a 79% accurate Naive Bayes classifier.

## Existing Model for Leather Defect Detection

Over the past ten years, numerous machine-vision-based methods for inspecting surface imperfections, including surface imperfections in leather, have been developed. The two primary types of these techniques are machine learning, which is based on handcrafted features or shallow learning techniques, and traditional image processing. In machine learning-based approaches, feature extraction and pattern classification are typically combined. The defect-detection feature vector’s design is based on an examination of the input image’s characteristics. Visual review is emotional and can be affected by variables like lighting conditions and individual mastery. Image processing algorithms can be effective at detecting specific types of defects, but may struggle with variations in lighting or color.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which are based on deep learning, have demonstrated promising results for accurately identifying various leather defects. With more training data, these methods can get better over time, learn patterns, and analyze a lot of data.

## Proposed Leather Defect Detection using CNN

Defects in leather are analogous to flaws in the leather surface. The majority of leather defects are brought on by problems with machines or processes. The sale and use of textiles are greatly diminished when leather has defects. In order to continue expanding and remaining competitive, textile manufacturing businesses need to upgrade their technology and equipment. The image was converted to greyscale using the sharpening, median, smooth, binary mask, RGB extraction, histogram, and Sobel operator algorithms.

A Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) is a type of neural network that is mostly used to process images, classify, segment, and deal with other auto-correlated data. It has one or more Convolutional layers. Start with a straightforward CNN that has one hidden layer with approximately ten kernels in dimension 3 and one max pooling layer as a general rule to find damaged components and transmit them thru the microcontroller and store them in the IOT webpage. IoT (Internet of Things) can be highly relevant in leather defect detection by enabling real-time monitoring of environmental conditions such as temperature, humidity, and pressure.

## Working of leather detection:

1.  The initial step in leveraging the Internet of Things for defect detection involves installing sensors in the leather processing line, which can monitor various parameters such as temperature, humidity, and pressure. In order to ensure the ideal environmental conditions necessary for accurate defect assessment and prevention, leather defect detection necessitates the capture of pressure, humidity, and temperature.
2.  The sensor data can be collected and transmitted to a centralized server or cloud-based platform for processing.
3.  To enable real-time defect detection, the trained models can be deployed on edge devices such as cameras or sensors.
4.  The edge devices can capture images of the leather, which can then be sent to a central server for analysis.
5.  Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and other deep learning methods can be used by the central server to examine the images and spot any potential flaws.
6.  Upon categorizing the identified defects into various categories, a report can be generated to guide operators in taking the appropriate action.
7.  To optimize the production process and minimize wastage, the system can be integrated with other systems, including the production management system.
8.  By leveraging the data collected by sensors, the machinery used in the leather processing line can benefit from predictive maintenance.

## Conclusion

Due to the diverse nature of leather defects and the lack of annotated data for algorithm benchmarking, automated visual inspection faces significant challenges. Transfer learning and data augmentation techniques can improve performance on limited data, and CNNs can automatically learn features from raw data. The proposed leather defect detection system using CNN makes the process easier and simpler as the results of defects are communicated using IoT module directly to the administrators. This CNN-based defect detection method for finding flaws in blue wet leather defect detection using DL, produces high accuracy rates of up to 93.4%. The data set consists of near 1000 images and the experiment is done 6 to check the accuracy the data set consists of peepholes, folding of leather, etc. The experimental results show that detection of leather defect in earlier blue wet stage waives the processing cost and yields profits to manufacturers compared to other detecting methods which detect defect of completely processed leather. The future work will be extended by detecting the defects in the earlier stage of leather with fur using deep learning approach.

# Attack Detection for Stock Trading Application Using Unsupervised Machine Learning

V. Ajay Sam, Nikita Singh, S. Revathy, M. Shakeel, and S. Sathya Priya

Department of Computer Science & Engineering, Hindustan Institute of Technology and Science, Chennai, India.

E-mail: [ajaysam600@gmail.com](mailto:ajaysam600@gmail.com), [nikitasumo2000@gmail.com](mailto:nikitasumo2000@gmail.com), [srevathy@hindustanuniv.ac.in](mailto:srevathy@hindustanuniv.ac.in), [mohamed.shakeel14@gmail.com](mailto:mohamed.shakeel14@gmail.com), [sathyap@hindustanuniv.ac.in](mailto:sathyap@hindustanuniv.ac.in)

DOI: [10.1201/9781003430452-40](https://dx.doi.org/10.1201/9781003430452-40)

## Abstract

The use of stock trading applications are widespread among users and plays a crucial role in the global economy. Any attack or disruption in stock trading can incur serious consequences for businesses, investors, and the economy as a whole. The existing stock trading applications are collecting sensitive information from the users and storing it in their centralized servers which are vulnerable to various active attacks. The conventional supervised machine learning algorithms which are used to detect the attack in stock trading applications are only suitable to detect known attacks. To detect the unknown attack and to reduce the computational time of the attack detection, the One-Class Support Vector Machine (OCSVM), is an unsupervised machine learning model with feature discretization and feature selection proposed. The model outperforms the existing model with an accuracy of 99.1% by reducing the computational time of attack detection by identifying and mitigating the potential threats against investors.

Keywords: Attack detection, One Class SVM, Stock trading, Unsupervised learning, Feature discretization

## Introduction

Numerous stock trading platforms gather all the sensitive and behavioral information of the users and store it in centralized servers. Supervised machine learning algorithms are used for detecting well-known attack types and their variants. The known and unknown attacks are only detectable by unsupervised machine learning techniques. In active attacks, the attacker tries to sabotage the message’s content by intercepting the connection. In the passive attack, the attacker spoofs the traffic information without causing damage to the network. The detection of attacks in the network is efficient when it detects with a higher accuracy rate and lesser computational time.

## Characteristics of Attack Detection

### Anomaly detection

Attack detection should be able to detect peculiar patterns of behavior and network activities that deviate from the normal pattern.

### Multi-level detection

The attack detection should detect intrusions at multiple levels, including network, application, and user levels, to ensure comprehensive coverage.

### Scalability

The attack detection should be able to manage vast volumes of data and scale up to meet the needs of a growing organization.

### Low false positives

The attack detection should have a low false positive rate to minimize the number of false alarms and allow security teams to focus on real threats.

### Integration

The attack detection should be able to integrate with other security tools and solutions to provide a comprehensive security framework.

To enhance the security and integrity of the stock market, a more efficient attack detection system is developed utilizing OCSVM along with feature selection and discretization techniques. The new system aims to address the limitations of the existing attack detection systems and enable quicker identification and mitigation of attacks. Its ultimate goal is to provide better protection to the stock market against potential security threats.

The structure of the paper is organized as follows, Section 2 covers the use cases of attack detection and 3 covers the related work of attack detection in stock trading, Section 4 illustrates the current attack detection model for stock trading, Section V provides the results and discussion of the proposed model, and Section VI provides the conclusion.

## Use Cases of Attack Detection

### Individual Investors

Individual investors can use attack detection systems to monitor their investments and protect themselves from financial fraud. By analyzing market data for anomalies or patterns that indicate an attack ([Zhang et al., 2017](#ch40.xhtml#ref40_7)), investors can adjust their investment strategies and avoid making costly mistakes.

### Hedge funds and Asset Managers

It relies on accurate and timely market data to make investment decisions. Attack detection systems can help these firms identify potential threats to their portfolios, such as market manipulation or insider trading, and adjust their investments accordingly.

## Regulators

Regulators such as the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) are responsible for monitoring the stock market for illegal activity ([Hu et al., 2018](#ch40.xhtml#ref40_12)) and ensuring that market participants follow the rules. Attack detection systems can help regulators identify potential violations of securities laws, investigate suspicious activity, and enforce compliance.

### Trading platforms

Trading platforms such as stock exchanges or electronic trading networks are responsible for maintaining a fair and orderly market. Attack detection systems can help these platforms identify potential threats to market integrity, such as algorithmic trading glitches or market manipulation, and take appropriate action to prevent further harm.

#### Financial news outlets

Financial news outlets rely on accurate and timely market data to report on stock market trends and provide analysis to their readers(F. Aslam and H.-G. Kang, 2015). Attack detection systems can help these outlets identify potential threats to market stability, such as sudden drops in trading volume or sharp price movements, and provide timely updates to their readers.

## Related Work

In the Network Anomaly Detection Algorithm solely analyses unlabeled data to identify traffic anomalies ([Casas et al., 2012](#ch40.xhtml#ref40_9)). By using the trace modification program called Flame, the authors have built many attack types to test the methodology ([Wagner et al., 2012](#ch40.xhtml#ref40_2)). Additionally, the true positive and average accuracy rates are insufficient to identify the intrusion in order to preserve the availability and confidentiality of the network resources. It is also necessary to evaluate false positive and false negative rates([Almseidin et al., 2017](#ch40.xhtml#ref40_8)) for attack detection. To identify attacks without any prior knowledge, the SSC-OCSVM unsupervised anomaly detection system coupled with one-class support vector machines and subspace clustering (Pu, et at., 2021). This algorithm’s use of feature selection has been successful in accelerating testing, although it will somewhat impair accuracy( \[L. [Hakim et al, 2019](#ch40.xhtml#ref40_6)). With the Kaggle dataset, supervised learning, which involves utilizing techniques such as Random Forest, Decision Tree, and Logistic Regression, is employed to make precise predictions about stock prices. This method relies on historical data from the preceding year and daily trading prices to forecast the stock prices of the target company ([Yelne and Theng, 2021](#ch40.xhtml#ref40_1)).

The market is highly unpredictable, and making forecasts based on disorderly and time-sensitive data is challenging, making stock movement prediction a difficult problem. Using a fresh stock movement prediction dataset, cutting-edge performance is proposed in the suggested model ([Xu and Cohen, 2018](#ch40.xhtml#ref40_11)). Artificial catastrophes and terrorism have drawn the public’s attention to how these events affect the economy and the stock market. This study investigates how natural disasters affect people ([Tavor and Teitler-Regev, 2019](#ch40.xhtml#ref40_10)). The above study brings out the challenges of the existing attack detection models by stating that unsupervised machine learning models are the finest for detecting unknown attacks. To reduce computational time, unsupervised learning can be integrated with feature selection and feature discretization methods.

## Proposed Attack Detection model

The various phases of the proposed attack detection model are illustrated in [Fig. 1](#ch40.xhtml#fig40_1).

[Fig. 1. Activity diagram of Attack Detection System](#ch40.xhtml#R_fig40_1)

## Initialization

Initialization phase involves setting up the necessary hardware and software, installing any required libraries or frameworks, and configuring the system to connect to relevant data sources. It is also important to ensure that the system is specifically engineered to effectively handle vast quantities of data efficiently and effectively since the stock market generates vast amounts of data daily.

## Feature Selection

Feature selection might involve identifying key market indicators, such as trading volume or price changes, that are likely to be affected by attacks. Different techniques can be used to select features, such as statistical analysis, domain expertise, or machine learning algorithms. The goal of feature selection is to decrease the complexity of data while obtaining as many relevant details as possible, which can improve the accuracy and efficiency of an attack detection system. Chi-square test has been an important phase in the feature selection method that identifies relevant features.

## Feature Discretization

Feature discretization involves dividing trading volume into high, medium, and low categories, or dividing price changes into positive, negative, or neutral categories. Different methods can be used for feature discretization, such as binning, clustering, or decision trees. The goal of feature discretization is to simplify the data while preserving important information, which can make it easier to detect anomalies and attacks.

## One Class Support Vector Machine (OCSVM)

One-class SVMs might be used to identify unusual patterns in trading volume, price changes, or other market indicators that could indicate an attack. One-class SVMs are trained on normal data and can identify outliers that are different from the normal patterns. They can be useful for detecting attacks that are not well-defined or for which there is limited training data.

## Attack Detection

Many different types of attacks can occur in the stock market, such as insider trading, market manipulation, or distributed denial of service attacks. Detecting attacks requires a combination of domain expertise, statistical analysis, and machine learning algorithms. Once an attack is detected, the system should alert users and provide them with relevant information, such as the type of attack, the time it occurred, and the potential impact on the market.

## Results and Discussions

The proposed attack detection model uses the NSL-KDD dataset. The following outcomes are attained using the supervised machine learning techniques like support vector machine (SVM), K-nearest neighbor (KNN), and random forest (RF), as well as our suggested method OCSVM with feature selection and feature discretization as illustrated in [Fig. 2](#ch40.xhtml#fig40_2). Recall is defined as the ratio of true positives to false negatives. Precision refers to the accuracy of detection of genuine attacks without false alarms. Calculating accuracy is done by dividing the total number of forecasts by the number of accurate predictions. The Recall, Precision and Fl score of the model is 98.3,99.7 and 99.1 respectively. The computational time of the model is reduced from 235s to 101s by the use of feature selection and discretization methods.

![Fig. 2. Efficiency of the Attack Detection Model](images/fig40_2_C.jpg)

[Fig. 2. Efficiency of the Attack Detection Model](#ch40.xhtml#R_fig40_2)

## Conclusion

The proposed attack detection system for stock trading applications using unsupervised machine learning has the potential to detect unknown attacks efficiently with accuracy of 99.1% and reduce computational time. It ensures investor confidence and prevents financial losses due to attacks. The efficiency is achieved by including the feature selection and feature discretization methods. Future research work will be extended by capturing real-time data from various sources to automatically detect potential attacks using machine learning.

# Manipulation of 3D Objects in Handheld Augmented Reality for Campus Virtual Visit

Motipalli Tharun, Romella Naveen, Muthukumaran Malarvel[^(32)](#fn32)

Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Hindustan Institute of Technology and Science, Chennai, India

DOI: [10.1201/9781003430452-41](https://dx.doi.org/10.1201/9781003430452-41)

## Abstract

This framework demonstrates how to control augmented reality objects (AR). By the use of AR technology, it is the interaction of virtual goods with the actual world. It tries to make manipulating digital information for users seamless and simple. Gestures, input devices, computer vision, and visuals are used in the manipulation. Using virtual objects of the buildings and rooms, we will develop a virtual campus visit within this framework. This framework aids observers in comprehending a building’s elements and architecture. This suggested model explains how buildings and architecture are organized and can be useful as a virtual tour for the spectator. In this paper, we are using object tracking and Marker-Based Tracking in this framework. This paper aims to give a framework that can be used for a virtual tour of the campus by creating a better user experience.

Keywords: Augmented Reality, Computer Vision, Object Manipulation, Object tracking

## Introduction

Handheld augmented reality (AR) has grown in popularity over the past several years across many industries, including education and travel ([Yu et al., 2019](#ch41.xhtml#ref41_9)). With the growing use of smartphones and tablets, handheld augmented reality offers an engaging and immersive way to experience both the physical and digital worlds at once. Virtual campus visits, ([Voutos et al., 2022](#ch41.xhtml#ref41_1); [Zhigang et al., 2021](#ch41.xhtml#ref41_2); [Cao et al., 2021](#ch41.xhtml#ref41_3); [Sundarramurthi et al., 2022](#ch41.xhtml#ref41_4); [Kondlo et al., 2020](#ch41.xhtml#ref41_5))which let potential students or visitors experience a university campus more interestingly and educationally, are one possible use of handheld AR. The manipulation of 3D objects in handheld AR for virtual campus tours is still difficult, though. In this study, we offer a unique method for manipulating 3D objects in handheld AR for virtual campus tours (Jacobe et al., 202)as a response to this problem. Our method takes advantage of portable devices’ capabilities and augmented reality (AR) technologies to build a simple and user-friendly interface for engaging with virtual items on a college campus. We think that our strategy could improve the visitor experience and encourage university campus participation.

It has been demonstrated that augmented reality in education improves learning results and student engagement ([Zhou & Tai, 2022](#ch41.xhtml#ref41_7)). AR can help students envision and comprehend abstract ideas more concretely by offering an interactive and immersive experience. Additionally, a number of school-related activities, including campus tours, orientation sessions, and student recruitment events have made use of augmented reality (Jacobe et al., 2021).

The difficulty of naturally and intuitively engaging with 3D items in these settings is one obstacle to the implementation of augmented reality. Traditional AR interfaces frequently rely on touch gestures or other challenging to learn and master input techniques ([Schmetz et al., 2019](#ch41.xhtml#ref41_15)). However, recent developments in computer vision and machine learning have made it possible for new methods of manipulating 3D objects in augmented reality, including voice commands, gaze tracking, and hand tracking ([Sundarramurthi et al., 2022](#ch41.xhtml#ref41_4)). It describes a novel method for manipulating 3D objects in handheld augmented reality for virtual campus tours ([Voutos et al., 2022](#ch41.xhtml#ref41_1); [Zhigang et al., 2021](#ch41.xhtml#ref41_2); [Cao et al., 2021](#ch41.xhtml#ref41_3); [Sundarramurthi et al., 2022](#ch41.xhtml#ref41_4); [Kondlo et al., 2020](#ch41.xhtml#ref41_5)). Our method combines hand tracking and an intuitive way to interact with virtual items. Through a user study, we assess our strategy in addition to contrasting it with conventional touch-based interaction techniques ([Schmetz et al., 2019](#ch41.xhtml#ref41_15)). We think that our strategy can greatly improve user experience and raise interest in virtual campus tours.

Here in these above papers, the authors have worked on different technologies and methodologies. In this paper, we will be using Marker-Based Tracking for virtual campus experience.

The remainder of this essay is organized as follows. A summary of some of the literature to which we have made references is provided in Section 2. In Section 3, the suggested system and modules are shown and discussed. We present the Results and Discussion in Section 4. In Part 5, we come to some conclusions and future work and go over some potential next steps.

## Literature Survey

Jacobe et al., (2021) propose a mobile application that utilizes augmented reality (AR) to enhance the tourism experience at the Wari Willka Museum in Peru. The authors begin by discussing the limitations of traditional museum experiences as well as the potential benefits of AR-based systems in providing visitors with a more engaging and interactive experience. They then describe the development of their mobile application, which allows visitors to access AR content such as virtual tours, 3D models, and multimedia presentations using their smartphones. [Zhou & Tai, (2022](#ch41.xhtml#ref41_7)) proposes a solution for enhancing museum visits through the use of smart augmented reality technology. The authors propose a smart augmented reality self-guiding application that uses a smartphone or tablet to display 3D models and animations, as well as provide audio and text descriptions of exhibits. The augmented reality technology enables visitors to interact with the exhibits and learn about them in a fun and engaging way.

[Bakhmut et al., (2021](#ch41.xhtml#ref41_8))in their study, in order to enable virtual campus tours created an AR- based web application. The authors overlaid 3D models of campus structures and landmarks on real-world images taken with a smartphone camera. They did this by using image recognition and tracking technology. Each location’s historical and cultural value was also covered in the application’s supplemental material. [Yu et al., (2019](#ch41.xhtml#ref41_9))in their study focused on developing techniques for natural and intuitive manipulation of 3D virtual objects in AR environments, specifically on handheld devices. The main goal of the study is to design a system that takes into account the effects of gravity in AR and provides a smooth, seamless user experience for object manipulation. The study likely employs computer vision techniques for tracking and interpreting the user’s hand movements and gestures, as well as machine learning algorithms for predicting the user’s intention and determining the desired manipulation.

[Li et al., (2021](#ch41.xhtml#ref41_10))investigate the use of machine learning techniques for manipulating objects in augmented reality in their paper titled “Object Manipulation in AR Using Machine Learning Techniques” (AR). Traditional AR interfaces for object manipulation, such as touch or gesture- based methods, the authors argue, can be limited in functionality and intuitive use. To address this issue, the authors propose training the AR system with machine learning algorithms to recognize user intentions based on their movements and actions in the AR environment.

[Wieland et al., (2021](#ch41.xhtml#ref41_11))in their study, describe the comparison of three collaborative 3D object manipulation techniques for handheld augmented reality: separation, composition, and hybrid is the focus of the paper. According to the study’s findings, the hybrid technique was the most efficient in terms of task completion time and error rate, while the composition technique was the most effective in terms of number of interactions

[Yang et al., (2021](#ch41.xhtml#ref41_12))in their study propose a deep neural network-based method for augmented reality object manipulation in real- time. The proposed method entails training a deep neural network to predict the virtual object’s transformation parameters based on hand movements captured by the AR device. The authors go into great detail about the network architecture and training process, including how they used a large-scale dataset and data augmentation techniques to improve the network’s accuracy. [Fang & Hong, (2021](#ch41.xhtml#ref41_13)) is an analysis of existing research in the field of augmented reality (AR) and its applications for interactive assembly tasks. The survey focuses on the use of bare-hand gestures for controlling virtual objects and the consideration of occlusions in AR systems. The survey aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state-of-the-art in the field, including the various hand tracking and gesture recognition techniques used in AR interaction, the methods used to handle occlusions and the results of user studies and evaluations of AR assembly systems.

The Study by Fazliaty Edora Fadzli et al. on the topic ([Nor'a et al., 2020](#ch41.xhtml#ref41_14))is an analysis of existing research in the field of handheld augmented reality (AR) and its applications for 3D manipulation using fingertips interaction. The survey aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state-of-the-art in the field, including the various techniques used for tracking and recognizing fingertips, the methods used to implement 3D manipulation using fingertips, and the results of user studies and evaluations of these systems.

The study by [Schmetz et al., (2019](#ch41.xhtml#ref41_15)) is focused on exploring and evaluating different methods for marking and annotating production parts using touch-based AR technology. The main goal of the study is to determine which touch-based AR marking techniques are most effective, efficient, and usable for industrial applications. The study likely involves a comprehensive literature review of existing research on touch-based AR marking, including both academic and industrial sources.

## Proposed System

### Design of the Model

First, we plan on gathering some 3D objects and the next step would be creating the 3D models in blender. Blender is a powerful and flexible 3D modeling tool that can make the process easier. In this framework, we’ll go through using Blender to create 3D models for augmented reality (AR) apps.

Before starting, it’s important to understand the requirements of the AR application you are working on. This includes factors such as the target device, the resolution and scale of the 3D models, and the specific features and animations needed for the AR experience. Once you have a clear understanding of these requirements, you can start creating the 3D models in Blender.

In the aforementioned [Fig. 1](#ch41.xhtml#fig41_1) the 3D models are constructed. Here are the models for the staff room, conference room, and block building are shown in [Figs. 1 (a—c)](#ch41.xhtml#fig41_1), respectively. UV mapping and adding textures will be applied next. While UV mapping is used to specify how the textures are applied to the models’ surfaces, textures aid to give 3D models depth and realism. A variety of UV mapping and texturing techniques are available in Blender, including the capacity to paint directly onto 3D objects and produce unique textures.

![Fig. 1 3D models](images/fig41_1_C.jpg)

[Fig. 1 3D models](#ch41.xhtml#R_fig41_1)

**After the 3D models are created and textured, the final step is to export them in a format that can be used in the AR application. Blender offers a range of export options, including popular 3D file formats such as .fbx and .obj. It’s important to ensure that the exported models are optimized for the target device and that any necessary animations or interactions are preserved in the export process.**

### Overview of System Architecture

Three layers make up the system architecture, which is how the framework operates. the output layer, the database layer, transition layer, and the recognition layer. These stages are crucial to the operation of the application. Vuforia and Unity are the tools we’re employing in this framework to create the application.

The suggested method for manipulating 3D objects in handheld augmented reality for virtual campus tours makes use of a modular system architecture to enable flexible and scalable implementation. An object database for 3D objects, a marker detection and tracking module, and a user interface module make up the architecture’s three core parts. The marker detection and tracking module use computer vision techniques to identify and follow physical markers in the user’s environment, giving the AR system precise position and orientation data.

A 3D object database, which houses the virtual representations of the campus buildings, landmarks, and other items, serves as the system’s brain. Also, the user’s location and orientation are determined via a marker-based tracking system, which is then utilized to overlay the necessary virtual items onto the actual surroundings The technology also has a visual guiding and feedback layer that the user may access while on the virtual visit. The suggested architecture offers a flexible and scalable framework for incorporating augmented reality (AR) in campus virtual visits by segmenting the various system components into independent layers.

There are many levels in the proposed architecture diagram shown in [Fig. 2](#ch41.xhtml#fig41_2), including the output layer, the database layer, and the recognition layer.

![Fig. 2 The Proposed System Architecture](images/fig41_2_8_C.jpg)

[Fig. 2 The Proposed System Architecture](#ch41.xhtml#R_fig41_2)

Recognition Layer: The system’s recognition layer, which uses system input and output, is a crucial part of the whole system. The GPS and camera on a mobile phone act as system input sensors, and the screen displays the overlay visuals. The user’s present position in respect to nearby points of interest is ascertained by the GPS while the AR markers are scanned by the camera. The program shows details about a location of interest while the user is walking by and is within proximity to it.

Database Layer: Data management, which includes data input, storage, and processing, is handled by this layer. Live data from the sensor layer is processed in this layer. Databases are used to hold details about numerous structures and tourist attractions at this tier. This paper’s processing unit is the Vuforia AR server, which is housed in the Cloud.

Transition Layer: In our application, this layer manages the change from one scene to another. Using 2D and virtual buttons, scenes are transitioned from one to the next. Because canvas is used to create 2D buttons. In an AR scene, virtual buttons are used.

Output: The output portion is obtained from the database once image processing is finished or when points of interest have been located. The result will be a screen presentation of the superimposed data on the user’s mobile device.

The campus map is employed in this framework, and the buildings and labs can be seen in augmented reality. In this framework, 2D Buttons are utilized in a Scene made up of a main camera, a direction light, and a canvas for showing the map.

A campus map and a few UI buttons for the framework. There are buttons for opening and exiting the app as well as buttons for showing various items. Two distinct segments make up the transition between scenes. Virtual buttons are used to exit the augmented reality environment and return to the map scene. UI buttons cannot be used in an AR scenario. Scene modifications and functionality may be provided through C# scripts. Functionalities may be defined using scripts, and other features can be added using a variety of assets. The items could be given additional textures to increase visibility.

### System Implementation

The application was created with an agile process. Images of different structures and laboratories are chosen and added to an online database. The AR mobile application was created with the help of Unity and the Vuforia SDK. This project’s scope was limited to Android-enabled mobile devices and was created with the Android SDK.

The Vivo V20 mobile phone was selected for testing due to its impressive specifications. It boasts a high-resolution display of 2400x1080, which provides a clear and vivid visual experience. The V20’s main camera has a 64MP sensor with a 26mm focal length and an aperture of f/1.9, allowing it to take clear, detailed pictures in a range of lighting situations. Additionally, the V20 is powered by a Snapdragon 720G processor and 8 GB of RAM, ensuring that the AR app can run smoothly and without any processing bottlenecks. Overall, the Vivo V20 is a reliable and powerful device that is well-suited for AR applications.

## Results and Discussion

We used a mixed-methods approach in this study to assess the usefulness of portable augmented reality for virtual campus tours. The survey involved a set of questions to analyze the user understanding of the application. They are

*H1. what do you think about the detailing and view of the virtual campus experience?*

*H2. what do you think about the user experience on interaction with virtual objects?*

*H3. what do you think about the interaction of the buildings, rooms and the manipulation of them like scaling and rotation?*

We recruited SO volunteers from the public for the full-scale study, which included people between the age of 21 to 35. Participants were chosen based on their interest in virtual campus tours and their knowledge of portable augmented reality technologies. We employed a portable augmented reality application named “Virtual Campus Tour” designed expressly for this study for study. Using a combination of 3D models and real-time video, the program was created to present users with an immersive and interactive virtual tour of a university campus.

We gathered both quantitative and qualitative data for the pilot research. A survey was distributed to participants before and after the virtual campus tour to obtain quantitative data. The survey included Likert-scale and open-ended questions intended to evaluate the user experience and efficacy of the portable augmented reality technology. Interviews with participants were performed immediately following the virtual campus tour to acquire qualitative data. For the full-scale study, we collected quantitative data through the same survey used in the pilot study, as well as through a series of usability tests. Usability tests were conducted with a subset of participants and consisted of a series of tasks designed to assess the ease of use and functionality of the handheld augmented reality application.

Images of the survey responses recorded for Questions H1, H2, H3 and graph of their distribution are observed in [Figs. 3(a—c)](#ch41.xhtml#fig41_3). A significant degree of user satisfaction was evident in the results, with 90% of participants saying that the model enhanced their virtual visit experience. 85% of participants found the marker-based tracking system to be user-friendly and accurate in determining their position and orientation, which speaks volumes about how well-liked it was. 80% of participants said that using touch-based interaction techniques was intuitive and simple, which contributed to its popularity. Overall, the poll results show the value and promise of our suggested approach for integrating portable AR to improve the virtual campus visit experience.

![Fig. 3 Response graph of the users](images/fig41_3_C.jpg)

[Fig. 3 Response graph of the users](#ch41.xhtml#R_fig41_3)

## Conclusion

This study’s goal was to create an Augmented Reality-based virtual tour guide (AR). This would make campus tours available without a guide. Throughout campus, AR markers have been placed at points of interest. Anybody with a capable mobile phone who has downloaded the necessary software may simply scan the markers with their phone. camera to discover the campus’s unique spots.

To give customers a smooth and interesting virtual visit experience, the model integrates a marker-based tracking system, a 3D object database, and intuitive interaction approaches. The success and potential of the suggested model were shown by the online survey results, with users indicating high levels of satisfaction with the system’s usability, accuracy, and utility. Further research in this field may entail extending the model to include more sophisticated interaction methods, including gesture recognition or haptic feedback, as well as connecting the system with other campus resources, like course schedules or campus maps. Overall, the suggested paradigm shows promise for utilizing portable AR to improve the virtual campus visit experience. While only compatible with Android smartphones, the program will eventually support iOS devices as well. Future additions could include the inclusion of tools like text-to-speech and navigation

# Locality Recommendation System Using Exploratory Data Analysis and Affinity Propagation

Abhishek Varma, Leela Krishna and Muthukumaran Malarver[^(33)](#fn33)

Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Hindustan Institute of Technology and Science, Chennai, India

DOI: [10.1201/9781003430452-42](https://dx.doi.org/10.1201/9781003430452-42)

## Abstract

In recent decades, the recommendation system is widely used in the field of location findings, online retail shops, real estate, healthcare, etc., The available methods are providing satisfactory performance. however still, the research is being proposed. Therefore, in this paper, we proposed a new model for location recommendation. Generally, a location recommendation system provides a suggestion to the users to find appropriate locations based on preferences. The user might like to settle in a specific neighborhood depending on elements like distance to a road, a mall, and other features. For example, if we take google maps as an example, it just provides a map view of locations and directions, but it cannot show a specific area or region where all the user’s preferences are met. To fill that gap, we have developed a model which recommends locations by taking personalized user and Context-Aware Recommendations like climate and weather conditions using geolocation plotting. This paper presents a detailed methodology for the development of the proposed system including the way of approach, usage of Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA), and implementation of affinity propagation algorithm.

Keywords: Recommendation system, Exploratory Data Analysis, Affinity Propagation, Geolocation plotting, context-aware recommendations

## 1 Introduction

Location recommendation systems ([Pan et al., 2022](#ch42.xhtml#ref42_1))provide suggestions to users about the most suitable locations for various purposes. These systems use various algorithms and techniques such as data mining, deep learning ([Dellal-Hedjazi & Alimazighi, 2020](#ch42.xhtml#ref42_2)), machine learning ([Fanca et al., 2020](#ch42.xhtml#ref42_3)), and geographic information systems (GIS) ([Xiaofang et al., 2007](#ch42.xhtml#ref42_4)) to recommend locations based on user preferences and historical data. Finding the right location using a recommendation system is a challenging task. Location recommendation systems can be used in various domains such as travel, food, entertainment, and many more. They can also be integrated into other applications such as maps, search engines, and e-commerce platforms to provide more relevant results.

The purpose of our developed model is to provide a more personalized and personalized and efficient experience to users which saves them time and effort in finding the right locality. The current recommendation systems for locality are often based on ratings and reviews, which may not be reliable and personalized. Additionally, these systems do not consider contextual factors that may affect user preferences such as weather and climate conditions. Therefore, there is a need for a more sophisticated approach that utilizes data analysis and machine learning techniques to provide accurate and personalized recommendations.

This proposed model aims to provide users with a more personalized location by utilizing the Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) technique ([Lee & Lee, 2022](#ch42.xhtml#ref42_5))and Affinity Propagation algorithm ([Tang et al., 2022](#ch42.xhtml#ref42_6)). The system will take into consideration various factors such as user preferences, weather, and climate conditions to provide accurate and relevant recommendations. The use of EDA will help in gaining insights into the data and identifying patterns and relationships between different factors. Affinity Propagation, on the other hand, will help in clustering similar data points and providing the final recommendations based on the most suitable cluster.

The method and strategy utilized to generate suggestions are what sets the proposed system apart from the existing model. Current location recommendation models frequently rely on straightforward techniques like content-based filtering or K-means clustering ([Saini et al., 2022](#ch42.xhtml#ref42_7)). These approaches might only work for certain people, but they are not always customized to the requirements and preferences of the person. The suggested system makes use of sophisticated data analysis methods to give users a more detailed and personalized location recommendation experience.

## 2 Literature Survey

Geo-locational data is a rapidly growing field of study that has revolutionized the way we understand the world around us. With the proliferation of Global Positioning System (GPS)- enabled devices and the ubiquity of location- based services, we are generating vast amounts of geo-locational data every day. However, analyzing and making sense of this data presents a unique set of challenges. The development of effective recommendation systems has become increasingly important for businesses seeking to enhance customer satisfaction and loyalty. The following literature provides a detailed discussion of various recommendation systems proposed earlier.

[Sumithra et al., (2022](#ch42.xhtml#ref42_8))proposed a methodology for finding accommodations and lodging using K-Means Clustering that would categorize accommodation for travelers according to individual choices for facilities, affordability, and proximity to the location to find the best choice.

[Kishan et al., (2022](#ch42.xhtml#ref42_9) )proposed a recommendation model to identify the most suitable lodging for an individual in a destination of a precise location by categorizing lodging for the people according to their choices of facilities and spending plans. It entails applying Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering to segment population and spatial information, which would be decided to apply on the geo-locational data obtained from REST API in classifying temporary accommodation for the people in full compliance with their priority areas.

[Pandya et al., (2016](#ch42.xhtml#ref42_10))involved in the development of a novel hybrid approach that combines clustering and association rule mining to overcome data sparsity and cold start problems in recommendation systems. Their approach clusters the rating matrix based on user similarity and applies the clustering Algorithm on Boolean data generated from the clustered data to efficiently generate rules.

[Xu et al., (2022](#ch42.xhtml#ref42_11))were involved in exploring the recent research on mini-batch AP clustering algorithm by focusing on the main approaches used, the advantages and disadvantages of the method, and the applications in various domains.

[Ma et al., (2020](#ch42.xhtml#ref42_12))implemented a POI behavioral change model based on the LBSN methodology. various kinds of information were integrated: customer check-in data, attribute data, spatial impact of POIs, and proximity of Objects. The Foursquare databases were used to carry out the study. The study showed that the factorization method achieves greater accuracy than other contemporary approaches.

[Li et al., (2020](#ch42.xhtml#ref42_13)) have proposed a two-stage clustering technique called DDAP in order to enhance the effectiveness and functionality of affinity propagation clustering and density curves. The suggested approach chooses a limited number of possible exemplars using the two variables of each cluster center in order to minimize the dimension of the similarity measure, and then it performs message-passing on the partial similarity matrix.

[Bandi et al., (2020](#ch42.xhtml#ref42_14))presented a brand-new method for dynamically categorizing textual Big Data that draws inspiration from Enhanced Learning and Segmentation approaches. This method can prepare the data for machine learning with few manual tasks and deliver great insights.

[Park et al., (2020](#ch42.xhtml#ref42_15))created a technique to group the RRHs using a customized form of the affinity propagation clustering algorithm in order to enhance the combined distribution of radio remote heads in densely packed tiny cellular systems.

[Panwar et al., (2021](#ch42.xhtml#ref42_16))suggested a methodology using machine learning to develop a recommendation engine utilizing big data within the framework of an e-commerce platform and also to provides valuable insights into the subject of data exploration. The research contribution begins by outlining the methods and techniques employed directly in sentiment classification often known as opinion mining.

[Banerjee & Chowdhury (2021](#ch42.xhtml#ref42_17))were involved in developing a method to study the relationship between reviews and textual and non-textual parameters in user-based analysis. They have analyzed two different datasets from Zomato and Yelp which have geographical differences and diverse user reviews. The authors have applied feature engineering and supervised and ensemble machine learning algorithms such as Linear regression, Logistic regression, XGBoost, and Gradient Boosting algo to construct a predictive model.

Here, in these above papers, the authors have worked on different technologies like clustering and classification, data analysis, filtering, and many more. For the location recommendation, they have used a hierarchical clustering model. In this paper, we are using an affinity propagation algorithm to overcome the limitation of low accuracy with non-spherical clusters.

## Proposed Methodology

This proposed system aims to provide users with a more personalized location by utilizing the Exploratory Data Analysis technique and Affinity Propagation algorithm. The system will take into consideration various factors such as user preferences, weather, and climate conditions to provide accurate and relevant recommendations. The Affinity propagation algorithm is used to discover the ideal area based on chosen choices for climate conditions, crime rate, amenities, budget, and proximity to the place and EDA is used for data visualization.

Affinity Propagation (AP) algorithm is a clustering algorithm that uses a message-passing approach to identify exemplars or prototypes that represent clusters. The algorithm is based on the concept of “similarity” and “responsibility” between data points, which are represented by matrices. Here is the equation for the AP algorithm. Similarity Matrix *S (u ,v)* represents the similarity or preference of point *u* to be an exemplar or prototype for point v . It is calculated based on the similarity between pairs of data points. The equation is presented in Eq. (1).

(1)  
*S*(*u*, *v*) =  − *d*(*u*, *v*)  

where *d* (*u,v)* is the Euclidean distance between point *u* and *v*. The negative sign is used to convert the distance measure to a similarity measure. Responsibility matrix *R(u ,v)* represents the accumulated responsibility that points *u* assigns to point to be an exemplar or prototype.

(2)  
*R*(*u*, *v*) = *S*(*u*, *v*) − max \[*a*(*u*, *k*) + *S*(*u*, *k*)\]*f**o**r* *a**l**l**k*! = *v*  

where *a(u ,v )* is the availability matrix that represents the accumulated availability that points v assigns to point *u* to be an exemplar or prototype.

(3)  
$$a(u,v) = \\min\\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{l} {0,R(v,u) + sum\\lbrack\\max(0,R(k,v))\\rbrack} \\\\ {for\\ allk! = uandk! = v} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack$$  

Availability matrix *A(u ,v ) -* It represents the accumulated availability that points [v] assigns to point /⁴ to be an exemplar.

(4)  
$$\\begin{array}{l} {A(u,v) = \\min} \\\\ {\\lbrack 0,R(u,v) + sum\\lbrack\\max(0,R(k,v))\\rbrack\\, for\\ allk! = u\\rbrack} \\\\ \\end{array}$$  

The AP algorithm iteratively updates the responsibility eq (1) and availability eq (2) matrices until convergence is reached. The exemplars are identified based on the diagonal values of the responsibility matrix. We are using the Affinity propagation algorithm over the k-means clustering in this paper. In this, each data point communicates with every other data point by telling them how desirable each target is to the sender comparable to the other proportional point. So, it can overcome the major drawback of when two circular clusters centered at the same mean have different radii and fails if the clusters are not circular. The Affinity clustering algorithm works by constructing the similarity matrix and responsibility matrix. And the developed system considers user context-aware and interactive recommendations. Eqs. (3) and (4) are representing the availability matrix in different cases.

For example, the time of day, weather conditions, or the user’s current location, and users can rate locations or provide additional information about their preferences. These can improve the accuracy of the recommendations and make the recommendation process more engaging and user-friendly. And these are the following various steps involved in developing the proposed system.

[Figure 1](#ch42.xhtml#fig42_1) depicts the various stages involved in the development of a proposed system. It involves matrix construction as an intermediate step. In that, similarity matrix Eq. (1) is used to find the similarity between the data points.

![Fig. 1. Flow diagram of the proposed method](images/fig42_1_C.jpg)

[Fig. 1. Flow diagram of the proposed method](#ch42.xhtml#R_fig42_1)

### Step 1: Collection of Datasets from Kaggle

The first step is to obtain data sets from Kaggle, which is an online platform for data scientists and machine learning practitioners to access and share datasets. Various datasets like air quality index, temperature fluctuations, apartment prices, hotels, and restaurants are collected as a sample preference for user.

### Step 2: Using Pandas and matplodib library to clean data and visualize data.

Once the datasets have been collected, they need to be cleaned and prepared for analysis. This step involves removing any duplicates, correcting errors, and consistently formatting the data. After cleaning the data, it is important to explore it visually to gain insights and identify any patterns or trends. Boxplots are a useful visualization tool that displays the distribution of a dataset’s values, including the median, quartiles, and outliers.

### Step 3: Matrix Construction

The matrix includes rows for each neighborhood or locality and columns for various features such as crime rate, school quality cost of living, etc. Each cell in the matrix would contain a value for the corresponding neighborhood and feature.

### Step 4: Employ affinity propagation clustering algorithm to duster the locations.

Next step is to use the Affinity propagation clustering algorithm that automatically determines the number of clusters and their centroids based on the data’s similarities by using scikit-learn library.

### Step 5: Get geolocational data points.

The next step is to obtain geolocational data points and coordinates for the localities in the dataset. This is typically done using the Foursquare API, which is a location data platform that provides access to a database of points of interest and user-generated content.

### Step 6: Display the resultant locations on the geolocational map using the Folium tool.

Finally, we can use Folium, a Python library for creating interactive maps to display the clustered locations on a geolocational map. This step allows us to visualize the different clusters and explore the relationships between them.

### Number of clusters is automatically assigned.

The user does not need to specify the number of clusters. In Affinity Propagation clustering algorithm, the number of clusters is automatically assigned based on the input data and the algorithm’s internal calculations.

### Allocate entities to each cluster.

The process of clustering involves assigning variables to each cluster. The easiest method is to cluster things at random, but this method may not always produce practical clusters. Depending on the nature of the data and the objectives of the research, the best approach for grouping things into clusters will be chosen.

## Conclusion

In conclusion, the proposed locality recom- mendation system that utilizes exploratory data analysis and affinity propagation clustering algorithm has shown promising results in identifying similar locations based on their characteristics and attributes. By using data collected from various sources and applying data cleaning techniques, the system was able to effectively cluster the locations and provide accurate recommendations based on user preferences.

Currently, there are various locality recom- mendation systems available that use different algorithms and techniques. However, most of them rely on collaborative filtering or content- based filtering to recommend localities to users. These systems have limitations in terms of accuracy, scalability, and sparsity of data. Also, they do not consider the user’s location, which is an important factor in recommending localities. The proposed system aims to overcome the limitations of existing locality recommendation systems by using exploratory data analysis and an affinity propagation clustering algorithm.

The use of geolocational data and mapping tools helped in visualizing the results and making them easily understandable for the users. Overall, the system has the potential to provide personalized and relevant recommendations for users looking for locations with similar characteristics by improving their overall experience and satisfaction. Further research and development can be done to improve the accuracy & scalability of the system and to incorporate additional features and data sources.

# Real-Time Pothole Detection Using Deep Learning

Sanchay Chakraborty, Dakshita Prashar and S. Sathya Priya[^(34)](#fn34)

Department of Computer Science and Engineering Hindustan Institute of Technology and Science Chennai, India

DOI: [10.1201/9781003430452-43](https://dx.doi.org/10.1201/9781003430452-43)

## Abstract

The detection and prevention of road accidents are a more complex and tough issue in India due to the use of subpar construction materials in the creation of road drainage systems. Owing to the aforementioned issues, roads deteriorate quickly and develop potholes, which result in accidents. The proposed work is to enhance safety by early real-time precise detection of potholes as it proves to be essential especially for emergency services like ambulances, firefighters and general public as well, especially in India where roads run for thousands of kilometres across the country. Road accidents claimed 1,53,972 lives and injured 3,84,448 people in the country in 2021, According to reports of 4,12,432 accidents, road accidents claimed 1,53,972 lives and injured 3,84,448 people in the country in 2021. Unfortunately, the age range most severely affected by road accidents is 18 to 45 years old, accounting for nearly 67 percent of all accidental deaths. According to studies, potholes and poor road conditions cause 60% of all road accidents in India. Without the necessary marking, many potholes are regularly neglected, and waterlogging prohibits the detection of any of these holes. In order to prevent accidents and fatalities brought on by badly maintained roads, harsh weather, late-night driving, and human error, road safety typically becomes a top concern at this time. The effectiveness of roads and the prevention of serious traffic accidents are both impacted by road maintenance surveillance. The proposed work would help to prevent loss of life and property by using You Only Look Once (YOLOv4), MIDAS, and adding an audio module to warn against potholes deeper than a particular depth.

Keywords: Deep Learning, MIDAS, Object detection, Pothole, Road safety

## Introduction

According to studies, 60% of traffic accidents are caused by structural problems and bad conditions of the roads. Today, roads are the primary form of transportation, and people rely heavily on them for daily travel. Due to heavy reliance on them as well as climatic changes, roads alter and deteriorate with time. This results in the formation of potholes and curved roadways, which are unsafe and cause life-threatening accidents. It is challenging to spot them on the road, particularly in a nation like India where there are thousands of kilometers of roadways. Since these potholes can’t always be located and examined by bare sight, automated detection of them is required. It is extremely important for a safe ride because even minor jerks or the invisibility of these potholes can prove to be extremely dangerous and fatal, especially for emergency services like firefighters and ambulances that operate at high speeds 24 hours a day, even in darkened areas and harsh weather conditions like fog and rain. Some current models identify potholes using different approaches, but they are not shown to be very efficient. As a result, a work is proposed that integrates an audio module, YOLOv4, and MIDAS for finding pothole deeper than a particular depth by making a buzzing sound as the car approaches them and notifying the driver and vehicle.

The suggested study can be used for both manual and self-driving vehicles, and the model is anticipated to demonstrate greater precision and accuracy for improved safety. YoloV4’s high accuracy makes it a great choice for finding potholes: Because of its smart architecture and improved training process. YOLOv4 is built on a more sophisticated architecture than YOLOv3 and SSD Mobilenet V2, it has a larger backbone network and used CSPDarknet53 which is better than traditional residual connections. Several convolutional layers and residual layers make up CSPDarknet53. It has optimizing techniques such as squeeze-and- excitation (SE) and spatial pyramid modules, by recalibrating the feature maps with channel-wise attention, SE blocks are employed to enhance the network’s feature representation. SPP modules handle objects of several scales by integrating and extracting features from various scales.

The CSPDarknet53 architecture boosts the YOLOv4 model’s performance by expanding the network’s capacity and lowering its computational expense, which makes it better compared to YoloV3 and Mobilenet V2.YoloV4 is relatively easy to train compared to other object identification algorithms, which is important for customizing the system to recognize specific types of potholes in different circumstances.YoloV4 provides more choices for customizing the algorithm to specific applications, including the capacity to alter the anchor box sizes and the amount of training iterations.YoloV4 offers support for new features including dynamic convolution and mesh activation that improve accuracy and performance. In conclusion, YoloV4 outperforms MobileNet SSD and YoloV3 in terms of pothole identification thanks to improvements in accuracy, microscopic item detection, speed, customization possibilities, and support for new features.

## Literature Survey

Prakash & Sriharipriya (2022) trained and compared the YOLOX-nano model to several YOLO models, such as the YOLOv3, YOLOv4, and YOLOvS models. The test demonstrates that the YOLOX-nano model is more precise than any other model. The YOLOX dataset was formatted based on the COCO 2017 dataset. The pre-processed data collection, which has been assigned a specific folder, serves as the YOLOX model’s training input. The model was designed to find a single class of potholes. The model’s average precision was 85.6%, which was slower than other models’ inference rates but 24.06% higher than the YOLOvSm model’s value.

The works by Asad et al. (2022) state YOLOv4 and Tiny-YOLOv4 are the best-fit pothole detection models as it uses AI kit (OAK-D) on a single-board computer (Raspberry Pi) as an edge platform for pothole detection. The custom weights are converted into the OpenVino IR format to perform real-time detection on OAK-D and Raspberry Pi as host computers. However, the proposed method is not cost-effective.

According to the study of (Anandhalli et al., 2022), sequential CNN and YOLO are compared, with CNN requiring less training time than YOLO (anchor-Based) while preserving pothole detection performance. Object detection in CNN was carried out by Object Classification and Object Localization. This method failed to encode the position and object orientation.

According to [Egaji et al. (2021](#ch43.xhtml#ref43_4)), a sufficient amount of samples from roads and automobiles will be needed to conduct further analysis and develop more effective models that work effectively in a variety of circumstances.

The approach used by [Abhiram et al. (2021](#ch43.xhtml#ref43_5)) is a vibration-based technology that detects the hole and hump mechanically, as well as the severity of each. The paper is devoid of technical specifications and detailed methodology explanations. Furthermore, the work has insufficient experimental validation because it only navigates a four-kilometer road. The work lacks novelty and resembles Google Maps. At a 95% confidence level, the average accuracy for the five machine learning models, SVM, Naive Bayes, KNN, Logistic Regression, and Random Forest Tree. The manual recording of pothole events uses GPS and UNIX timestamp data. Due to poor object orientation and detection, training input from manual dataset collection is less reliable.

The work by [Peng et al. (2022](#ch43.xhtml#ref43_6)) emphasizes pattern representation and suggests three sets of numerical features for expressing road conditions. Three deep learning techniques—Deep Feedforward Network, Convolutional Neural Network, and Recurrent Neural Network— are also considered to solve the classification problem. RNN was discovered to be the finest. The Adam optimizer was used, and 10 internal nodes of the LSTM cell were selected. However, it is outside the purview of this research and has not been investigated to evaluate the performances of different RNN cells on the dataset presented.

The suggested technology, which combines infrared imagery and convolutional neural networks, can compete with the pothole detection techniques already in use (Anandhalli et al., 2022). Three distinct ratios are used for the training and validation dataset: 60:40, 80:20, and 90:10. The approach that is recommended by [Aparna et al. (2022](#ch43.xhtml#ref43_7)), uses a CNN-based ResNet model. This is the first time that pothole identification has been done using infrared imaging. But as the use of thermal imaging for pothole identification is a new concept, there is no pre-existing work in this direction to be compared.

## Proposed System

For the desired beneficial consequences, the acquired data is converted and put through several processes. The work’s entire process is depicted in [Fig. 2](#ch43.xhtml#fig43_2) in its entirety. From several sources, a dataset of 700 road pictures is gathered for both with and without potholes. The images were split between training and testing sets with an 80-20 split. To ensure data completeness, data preparation is done by converting pixel values to the range \[0, 1\] and handling missing data with a median filter. To maintain the spatial dimensions, the feature extraction is accomplished using 19 convolutional layers with 3x3 filters and 5 max-pooling layers with 2x2 filters. LeakyReLU activation functions are then applied with a 0.1 negative slope and additional padding. A binary cross-entropy loss function with an IoU threshold of 0.5 was used to train the YOLOv4 model. To broaden the training set, data augmentation methods are used including random flipping and rotation.

![Fig. 2. Depicts the visual comparison of performance measures between yoloV4, yoloV3 and SSD MobileNetV2.](images/fig43_2_C.jpg)

[Fig. 2. Depicts the visual comparison of performance measures between yoloV4, yoloV3 and SSD MobileNetV2.](#ch43.xhtml#R_fig43_2)

MIDAS (Monocular Depth Estimation via Adaptive Structural Loss) approach is utilized to measure the distance of potholes from the camera. Using the pinhole camera concept, the depth map created by MIDAS was transformed into actual distances. The technology was able to provide precise information about the location and severity of potholes thanks to distance estimation. For MIDAS normalization of pixel values is done to the range \[0,1\] and enlarge the input image to 256 x 256 pixels. The depth map is then obtained by running the normalized image through the MIDAS model. The pinhole camera model translates depth map to actual distances. It assumes that light moves in straight lines and that images are created by directing light rays from a scene’s 3D point onto a 2D picture plane. Use the following equation to get the separation between a point in the scene and the camera: distance = (focal length \* object height) / image height, while object height is the height of the object in the scene. It calculates the object’s coordinates by using the pothole’s coordinates as its bounding box, as detected by YOLOv4. Where focal length is the distance between the camera and the picture plane, object height is the height of the object in the scene, and image height is the height of the image in pixels. It calculates the object’s coordinates by using the pothole’s coordinates as its bounding box, as detected by YOLOv4.

Fig. 1. Block Diagram

## Results and Discussion

Experiments were conducted wherein a test set of 700 photos, YoloV4 has an average precision and recall of 0.85 and 0.91 respectively. The Fl score of 0.88 demonstrated a good level of pothole detection accuracy. Out of the 700 test photos, 95% were accurately identified as potholes or non-potholes. The YoloV4 model successfully detected potholes of various sizes, shapes, and lighting situations, showcasing its potential for use in practical settings. Future research might concentrate on enhancing the model’s robustness and accuracy in difficult conditions.

The YoloV4 model’s visual depiction demonstrates its higher accuracy, precision, and mAP compared to YoloV3 and SSD MobileNet V2.Yolov4 has advanced augmentation techniques like mix up data augmentation and cutmix data augmentation that are not present in YoloV3 and SSD MobileNet V2, which helps to increase the diversity and amount of training data and improves the accuracy of the model.

 Table 1 depicts the comparison of Yolov4 model with other models. 

 
| ALGORITHM  || ACCURACY || PRECISION || mAp |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| YOLOV4 || 0.95 || 0.91 || 80.08% |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| YOLOV3 || 0.89 0.90 || 65.05% |
| SSD MobileNetV2 || 0.63 || 0.75 || 41.83% |

According to the visual representation, YoloV4 performs better than YoloV3 and SSD MobileNet V2 across all evaluation measures, with higher values and more reliable outcomes. Advanced loss functions that are not included in YOLOv3 or SSD MobileNetV2 are used by YOLOv4, such as the focused loss function and the DIoU (Distance-IoU) loss function. These loss functions aid in addressing the problem of class imbalance and boosts the model’s accuracy in challenging situations, including spotting tiny potholes. YOLOv4 can be easily linked with distance estimation algorithms, such as MIDAS, to determine the distance of potholes from the car. This is crucial for warning drivers ahead of time that there will be potholes so they can prevent damaging their cars.

## Conclusion

Techniques for identifying potholes based on artificial intelligence could improve road maintenance, notably in India. Emergency services must take every precaution to avoid obstructions that could endanger their lives. This work is expanded to determine the place where the potholes are located after classifying a photo as a pothole. A driver can be warned by an alarm system to avoid uneven roads and avoid accidents by using factors like the depth and severity of the potholes that are discovered.The model showed very good accuracy and pothole identification in real time. The system’s usability and security were further improved by the incorporation of a sound alert system and distance measurement using MIDAS. The web application makes the model’s user interface accessible and makes it easier for people to apply it in practical situations. In future research, the pothole detecting system developed in this study might be improved even more by including GPS and other sensors to gather more data. Using GPS, the system would be able to more precisely locate potholes and provide drivers with more detailed information about the route ahead, including the condition of the road and traffic patterns.
